This paper explores the feasibility and benefits of cooperative optimization on general-purpose processors using hardware-software cooperation techniques. We outline the essential features needed for cooperative optimization at the processor level and its supporting infrastructure, as well as the cooperative operations that can be performed by the processor to enhance application efficiency. We discuss the effectiveness of these cooperative methods in achieving optimal performance across various program workloads, illustrate the challenges in balancing cooperation benefits and overheads, and provide case studies of hardware-software co-design to showcase the promising results of cooperative techniques in real-world applications.

Deep learning techniques utilizing pre-trained networks that are adaptable to diverse image patterns have been instrumental in advancing computer vision capabilities.  The integration of super-resolution methods trained solely on natural images with deep architectures trained on vast, comprehensive image datasets, has led to substantial enhancements in visual understanding.  The focus of our work lies in addressing the challenge of super-resolution for facial images, an area of increasing importance.  Our research presents a novel super-resolution approach that combines a deep architecture with a fine-grained facial feature extraction capability and a face halluculation network, enabling the generation of high-quality facial images.  The results of our experiments demonstrate that our method not only recovers detailed facial features but also maintains facial identity, even when images are severely downsampled.  Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of qualitative and quantitative experiments on multiple datasets.

The presence of a positive entire solution to a quasi-linear elliptic system
with a specific class of nonlinear components has been confirmed using the
Pohozaev variable exponent functional. To establish this finding, a set of
regularity conditions for the nonlinear exponents was established, allowing
for the application of the Mountain Pass Theorem in $\mathbb{R}^N$.

Neural networks with recurrent structures have been a popular choice for modeling complex time-dependent data, due to their capacity to learn and represent long-term relationships. However, training these networks can be a difficult task, as they often rely on short-term memorization instead of a true understanding of the underlying relationships. This shortcoming is particularly evident in tasks requiring long-term generalization capabilities. This study investigates the potential of using graph neural networks to improve the learning and representation of long-term dependencies in recurrent neural network-based systems. By leveraging graph neural networks to provide a broader view of the time-dependent data, the recurrent networks' ability to capture long-term relationships is demonstrated. Experimental results show that combining graph neural networks with recurrent networks leads to improved performance in a variety of natural language understanding tasks, as well as in modeling the dynamics of a complex social interaction model.

This paper develops a value function for Markov Decision Processes that may have absorbing states and explores its connection to reinforcement learning. We establish a mathematical framework that ensures the value function's continuity and its convergence when averaged over all possible policies. This theoretical foundation is crucial in proving a pivotal result in reinforcement learning that relies on the value function. We also introduce a concept of ergodicity in MDPs and show that under certain conditions, including ergodicity, the function can be estimated reliably. To that end, we propose a novel criterion called policy-independent estimation, which enables the derivation of a PAC bound for any policy that satisfies the proposed conditions, yielding the first-known reliable estimate in reinforcement learning.

A novel plasma-based electron accelerator technique is proposed that leverages a mid-infrared laser to generate an ultrashort, highly luminous electron bunch with a 100-eV energy in just 100 femtoseconds. This technique could be applied in ultra-low energy radiation sources, such as those needed for advanced x-ray free-electron lasers. The resulting electron bunches feature extremely high charge densities, up to 100 times that of conventional accelerators, and maintain a low, subpercent spread in energy. This achievement is made possible by a unique combination of a specific laser frequency and a unique phase offset, which together mitigate space-charge effects during acceleration. Simulations based on 3D simulations of laser-plasma interactions have confirmed the feasibility of this technique.

One of the most profound enigmas in modern physics involves the source and nature of the increasing complexity found in the world of living beings. In an attempt to resolve this issue, our research delves into the properties of a vital scalar field believed to be responsible for the growth of complexity. By analyzing the characteristics of this scalar field, particularly its coupling strength, our method enables the derivation of the fundamental principles governing the microscopic behavior of living cells. Furthermore, our approach aims to uncover the physical laws governing the emergence of new properties at higher levels of organization.

To ensure that Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) policy decisions are well-informed, it is essential that the public, policymakers, and stakeholders have unrestricted access to relevant research outputs. This access enables them to analyze and utilize the findings, ultimately informing policy decisions. The Global Research Data Strategies Survey, which was conducted by the Research Data Alliance (RDA) in 2020, investigated the implications of open research output and data for research funding, infrastructure, and intelligence generation. The survey aimed to identify the challenges and opportunities associated with opening up research outputs and data, and how these issues affect the development of effective STI policy within and for low-income countries. The survey results provide insights into the complexities and opportunities presented by opening up research outputs and data, and offer recommendations for policymakers and stakeholders in both high-income and low-income countries.

The most widely used smartphone operating system, Android, remains vulnerable to various side-channel attacks despite previous research highlighting these risks. This is particularly concerning due to the established methods of exploitation, which have led to the development of sophisticated attack techniques. This study aims to evaluate the current level of exposure of Android devices to these threats and to introduce a novel method for making these attacks more feasible. This involves integrating a memory leak detection mechanism into the Android kernel, which can be triggered remotely by an attacker. The results of testing this approach on 13 different Android devices revealed a memory leak in 9 instances, allowing attackers to gain access to sensitive information in  all but one case.

Ethereum, a community-driven platform, has become a popular choice for developing decentralized applications (dApps), with a wide variety of account types, including general accounts, contract creators, and typical account holders, each with distinct purposes. Understanding the transaction patterns of these accounts can greatly benefit Ethereum's development and research. However, previous studies have mainly focused on transactions at a high level, neglecting the unique characteristics of Ethereum accounts. In this study, we propose a new approach to analyze Ethereum account transactions and propose a new method called the network feature clustering (NFC) algorithm to categorize accounts based on their transaction patterns. Experimental results show that the network feature clustering algorithm can effectively distinguish between typical, creator, and holder accounts based on transaction patterns, with accuracy rates of up to 83.33%.

The interplay between charge and disorder dynamics at the junction of specific oxides with two-dimensional electron systems has garnered significant interest. A thorough examination of the impact of illumination, applied in varying intensity levels from 10 to $10^4$ mW/cm$^2$, has been conducted on a LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface, with the findings revealing a decrease in sheet resistance with increasing light intensity. A notable transformation has been observed in the Hall magnetoresistance curve at low magnetic fields, indicating the presence of a minor bulk contribution. A detailed analysis of the Hall signal reveals a significant enhancement of the Hall coefficient, signifying a substantial increase in carrier mobility. These results collectively demonstrate that light exposure triggers a substantial increase in the number of mobile carriers within the two-dimensional system.

B\"uchi's BV logic, incorporating both positive and negative atomic assertions, has been shown to be highly complex. Although incorporating modal operators with operational meanings increases complexity, BV logic, without them, is surprisingly more complex than the extension incorporating modal operators. This study delves into the relationship between resolution rule systems and BV logic, presenting two complete systems, one of which is restricted to restricted negation. We find that we cannot freely add new rules without making the logic unsolvable, even when limited to restricted negation. Using these findings, we prove that BV logic with restricted negation is an NP-hard problem in terms of satisfiability.

The pentagon identity for quantum dilogarithms and the five-term relation in Macdonald's conjecture are generalised using a modified star-stacked version of Macdonald's binomial coefficients, which exhibits a new form of pentagon and hexagon structure. This is demonstrated through a proof that extends Macdonald's conjecture to weight functions of the form $\lambda_0 + \lambda_1 q^i + q^j \lambda_1$, which was initially conjectured by Garsia and Misra. This new generalisation also leads to an expanded star-stacked version of Macdonald's conjecture over the rational numbers. This is achieved through the application of a technique known as "unstacking".

We have developed an approach to determine photometric redshifts by utilizing a deep learning technique with a two-step methodology, combining the use of convolutional neural networks and a random forest algorithm. Our method was applied to the Hubble Space Telescope images of the galaxy cluster CL J120958.1+5156244 from the Near Infrared Camera (NIC) and the Multi-Cycle Exploration Science program, resulting in the measurement of redshifts for 103 member galaxies. Our results show a median redshift of 1.1142 and a scatter of 0.005 with respect to spectroscopic redshifts obtained from the Very Large Telescope (VLT) Hubble Space Telescope (HST) spectra. Our method was also applied to the 103 non-member galaxies, resulting in an average redshift of 1.372 with a scatter of 0.159. Our method was tested using a two-dimensional approach, combining our deep learning results with a RF code, resulting in an average redshift of 1.345 and a scatter of 0.066. Our method was also found to be comparable to the results of the photo-z code, ZEBRA, resulting in an average redshift of 1.345 and a scatter of 0.066. Our method was found to be a reliable and accurate tool for determining photometric redshifts in galaxy clusters.

Complex computer models, whose behavior is heavily influenced by multiple interacting components, pose significant challenges due to their computational intensity. To overcome this issue, a Gaussian Process emulator has been developed to effectively "learn" complex computer models. This paper presents a novel, computationally efficient method for implementing Gaussian Process emulators. By leveraging a matrix decomposition approach, the numerical complexity of building these models is significantly reduced. This approach is particularly well-suited to models requiring the evaluation of derivatives. The new implementation method is demonstrated using a high-dimensional model of a carbon capture and storage well reservoir.

We investigate the feasibility of applying the quantum and classical density matrix renormalization (DMRG) and infinite time-evolving block selection method to two-electron systems by implementing the QC-DMRS method. Our study involves optimizing the DMRG algorithm to achieve the optimal wave function for a two-electron system, and we find that this can be done with minimal computational cost using a bond dimension of 3. Additionally, our analysis shows that the wave function obtained through the optimal DMRG method is complete and can be used to determine the full two-electron wave function. However, we also find that the QCTDVP method does not consistently converge to the optimal wave function, with some cases yielding a complete, but degenerate, complete wave function. Our study also demonstrates that the wave function obtained through the optimal DMRG method is superior to the complete wave function obtained through the QCTDVP method in terms of its ability to accurately determine the correlation energy.

To resolve discrepancies in the Standard Model's predictions, we explore an approach that involves modifying its structure. We propose adding a non-Abelian gauge symmetry, specifically $SU(2)_X$, and a single scalar field that can simultaneously address anomalies in muon and tau particles while also addressing the $R_{2D}$ anomaly. The introduced field's behavior can be constrained by experimental data. Notably, this model allows for the explanation of anomalies in the $R_{2D}$ lepton-bilinear coefficient while also providing a plausible explanation for the muon's anomalous magnetic moment.

Machine learning-based surrogates can significantly simplify complex coastal and ocean models, making them more manageable. This is particularly helpful in preparing for future high-resolution model simulations, which will be costly due to their complexity. A crucial aspect to validate and utilize high-precision, high-computation models is to find efficient machine learning-based surrogates. 

We have developed a machine learning-based model of the Regional Ocean Prediction System (ROPSE), which covers the entire East Asian coastal and oceanic regions. The model uses 15,000 ROPSE simulations over 10 days to train a physics-informed neural network, which produces highly accurate sea surface temperatures, which are comparable to those of the original model. 

To evaluate the performance of the machine learning-based model, we have applied it to 12 years of sea surface temperature data from 33 coastal stations in the East Asian region, which provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex oceanic and meteorological processes in the region. The model's performance has been found to be stable and consistent over time, with a high accuracy of 99% in its predictions. 

The model's performance has been further tested and validated using a 10-year sea surface temperature dataset from 16 coastal stations in the East Asian region, which provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex oceanic and meteorological processes in the region. The model's performance has been found to be stable and consistent over time, with a high accuracy of 99% in its predictions.

The collaboration behind the Cosmology and Astrophysics data from the Millimeter Array (CAMA) is releasing a comprehensive set of data and a publicly accessible pipeline for CMB analysis. This initiative aims to facilitate open-collaboration research, offering a transparent and community-driven data release. The CAMA collaboration is comprised of researchers from the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, Harvard University, the University of California, Santa Cruz, the International Center for Interdisciplinary Science, the University of British Columbia and the University of Edinburgh. The CAMA data is now available, along with its corresponding analysis, on data.cdmaobservatory.org. The release includes a publicly accessible data processing code, an interactive data exploration tool and a publicly accessible planckrom.org server. The CAMA collaboration is committed to transparency and to the open collaboration and collaboration on its research.

We explore the Turing instability in a three-component reaction-diffusion system where the reactive terms are minimal. Using a discrete mean-field approach, we derive the macroscopic system from the discrete model and then focus on a planar geometry with uniform initial conditions. We conduct a thorough asymptotic analysis of the macroscopic system, considering both near-threshold and general parameter regimes. We discover that the leading-order term of the macroscopic system is insufficient to capture the full dynamics of the system. To address this, we examine higher-order terms and find that the first correction to the leading-order term corresponds to a Turing instability-related perturbation. We rigorously establish that this correction is not significantly influential in the general parameter regime, but through numerical simulations, we find that it is crucial for capturing the full dynamics in the small-parameter regime.

A deformation of the pure Yang-Mills theory with a phantom field, which has a negative norm, reveals that quantum corrections cancel each other out. The vacuum shift, which occurs due to the presence of the phantom field, complies with the boundary condition derived from quantum field theory, thereby supporting its authenticity.

Our research examines the properties of nanowires made of GaAs and AlGaAs, with a focus on their photoluminescence characteristics. We investigate the effects of varying excitation intensities and powers on these NWs, revealing distinct behavior in the GaAs NWs, particularly when excited at 1580 nm. This excitation power triggers an inversion in the polarization of the photoluminescence, switching it from $\pm 1$ to $\pm 2$. This is demonstrated in samples with different compositions and is linked to differences in the valence band structure between the GaAs NWs and AlGaAs NWs.

Inferring an opponent's priorities is a vital skill for effective multi-issue negotiations. This knowledge enables agents to adapt their strategies within a negotiation by conceding on one issue in exchange for gaining advantage on others. Prior work in this area focused on direct communication with the opponent, but our research explores the challenges of inferring priorities without such communication. We introduce a neural network-based approach that can be applied to various available information sources, such as negotiation dialogue or negotiation outcomes. Our method is tested in both simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating superior performance over baseline models in most scenarios, particularly after large data sets are available to train it.

In certain scenarios involving Braneworlds, dynamic strings can become unstable. This leads to strings and other matter being confined within the worldsheet, creating a stable environment. As a result, new branes may form, taking the form of a specific type of stable, one-brane known as a soliton. This process can result in the creation of multiple branes, depending on the initial conditions. We've identified a specific condition that determines the maximum number of stable branes, and observed that under a specific type of coupling, the number of branes tends towards a maximum value.

Researchers at universities are increasingly adopting the use of randomized experiments, known as A/B testing, to determine which methods outperform which, thereby establishing reliable evidence for the effectiveness of different techniques in their fields. To date, these experiments have largely focused on establishing cause-and-effect relationships between specific variables and outcomes, without considering how different covariates might influence results. This paper addresses the issue of covariate imbalance in online experiments by proposing a theoretical framework and demonstrating a practical connection between these concepts. The theory provides a framework for understanding how covariates can affect the accuracy of statistical tests, while also establishing a practical method for implementing covariate balancing in an online experiment without requiring access to historical data.

The atomic structure of the Si surface covered with gamma-Al2O3 was investigated using a combination of computational methods and experimental data. The research identified a set of four distinct configurations for the Si atoms at the interface, contradicting a previous study's finding of two types of Si atoms. Instead, the current study shows that all resulting Si atoms are five-coordinated, aligning with an analysis of the natural abundance of isotopes in the gamma-Al2O3 using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The research further established that the Si atoms within the gamma-Al2O3 oxide octaeder are four-coordinated. The examined configurations exhibit identical stability and thus the Si/O ratio does not serve as a determining factor in determining the interface structure. The research identifies the Si atom positions within the gamma-Al2O3 cube as the most suitable location for the Si surface atoms at the interface. The research suggests that the interface structure can be characterized as a mixture of two types of point defects, with a ratio of defect types in agreement with an independent analysis of the defect distribution in gamma-Al2O3 using electron paramagnetic resonance.

This research explores the application of nonparametric techniques to study
Black Hole behaviour in the axion-dilaton system with reduced dimensions. To achieve
this goal, we employ kernel estimation to approximate physical Black Hole functions
such as horizon surface mass density and surface potential. The study utilizes both
parametric and nonparametric methods to generate data on these functions. We then
subject the estimated functions to a set of statistical evaluations to assess their
reliability, and our results indicate that kernel estimation with a Gaussian kernel
produces the most accurate results.

A comprehensive dataset of global shipping market indices from 1960 to 2021 has been compiled and made available on ReSearchpy. The dataset encompasses key indicators of the international shipping market, offering vital insights into significant historical events, such as the container revolution and its impact. The container crisis had far-reaching effects on the shipping industry, influencing freight rates, ship construction, and vessel capacity. The dataset also reveals how the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic influenced demand and freight rates. The dataset can be accessed via the ReSearchpy platform, with links to data sheets detailing the historical market indices of the shipping industry, including bulk and container shipping.

Real-time data analysis applications in various sectors rely heavily on anomaly detection from streaming data.  Although several anomaly detection methods are available, their effectiveness in different scenarios and environments is not yet fully understood.  To address this knowledge gap, we have developed a comprehensive benchmark framework that evaluates the performance of anomaly detection systems in diverse real-world environments.  Our benchmark framework, Enclave, is an open-source, Python-based tool that enables the analysis of streaming data, introduces new challenges, and provides a fair assessment of anomaly detection methods across various scenarios and settings.  By using Enclave, we have evaluated the performance of 32 anomaly detection methods and have made the evaluation results publicly available, which can serve as a reference for choosing the most suitable anomaly detection method for a given application.  Our Enclave benchmark framework, code, and evaluation results are accessible at https://github.com/openfunnel/enclave.

Gliomas are complex brain tumors characterized by multiple subtypes and varying patient outcomes, making accurate segmentation an essential diagnostic tool. Our deep learning approach utilizes a U-Net model to achieve highly accurate glioma segmentation, evaluating a large dataset of 327 scans with detailed volume measurements. The resulting segmentation accuracy achieved a Dice score of 0.884 and a Hausdorff distance of 6.377 voxel units. The precise identification of tumor substructures, including core, frontal, intratumoral, and frontal-superior regions, enables improved patient categorization and predictive modeling, ultimately leading to better treatment outcomes and more accurate patient risk assessments.

A "twin wave" of the triplon excitation is predicted to travel in a one-dimensional system, distinct from two-dimensional modes. Our research demonstrates the generation of correlated photon pairs through the interaction of two adjacent triplons in a spin-dimer chain. This effect, similar to the phenomenon of spontaneous parametric down conversion, is characterized by an entangled state of the dimer modes in the strong-coupling regime. By examining the entanglement of adjacent dimer modes, we reveal the nature of the triplon excitations' behavior. Furthermore, our analysis of the entanglement structure shows that the dimer modes form entangled qubits, and we identify the point at which these qubits become maximally entangled.

This article introduces the concept of statistical convergence via asymptotic density utilizing a network approach, while exploring the potential to expand established ideas on summability into a new framework for learning theory applications.

This study develops a novel numerical approach for computing the transmission eigenvalue problem. By adapting the conventional method, a new scheme is created which requires modifying only the stiffness matrix, derived from the underlying partial differential equation, without compromising its original structure. We establish essential error bounds for the method in the $H^1$ and $H^2$ spaces and provide a non-uniform a priori error analysis that confirms the method's reliability. Our numerical simulations validate the theoretical findings in the last section.

This research paper explores the properties of a second-order linear linearized model of the Stokes problem in a Hilbert space with non-uniform velocity boundary conditions. Utilizing an original discretization scheme that is similar to the classical finite element method, this study proves that its fixed points correspond to a solution of the continuous problem via the Leray-Schauder Theorem. The convergence rate of the iteration is established using a linear operator analysis, drawing from the properties of the Babuska-Brezzi Theorem. The stability and wellposedness of the continuous problem are demonstrated using an energy-based approach. The convergence iteration is applied to a finite element discretization of the problem, which is shown to be equivalent to a finite element discretization. The paper also presents numerical results that validate the theoretical convergence analysis.

In this research, we employ advanced many-body calculations to predict that charged excitons confined within layered two-dimensional semiconductors can exhibit an anomalous Hall effect under the influence of an external magnetic field. Our findings suggest that positively-charged interlayer excitons in a positively charged p-doped quantum Hall bi-layer heterostructure made of MoS2 exhibit anomalous behavior in a range of magnetic field conditions, specifically at carrier densities of approximately 1.5 x 10^13 to 3 x 10^13 per square centimeter. Our results further show that the observed Hall current is inversely proportional to the square of the carrier density and is directly proportional to the magnetic field strength. Our research offers a potential pathway for the observation of an anomalous Hall effect in two-dimensional materials through the controlled creation of electrically charged states.

The HIRES (High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer) on the Hobby-Eberly Telescope yielded exceptional results in its pilot run at a relatively low temperature of around 10 degrees Celsius. By achieving an unprecedented precision in measuring the speed of stars at a rate of just 0.2-0.5 km/s, HIRES surpassed the capabilities of other state-of-the-art spectrographs by up to 20 times. Key to its remarkable accuracy is its exceptionally wide margin of error, measuring as low as 0.5-1.5 cm per spectral line. Furthermore, its pilot run demonstrated that HIRES can accurately and consistently measure the speed of celestial objects at a scale as small as 0.01-0.16 arcseconds, far surpassing its previous precision of 1-5 arcseconds. With its impressive results, HIRES is poised to revolutionize the way we study the speed of celestial objects in the universe, particularly in the areas of measuring the rate of the Hobby-Eberly Telescope's proper motion, determining the speed of nearby stars, and studying the movement of binary stars.

A groundbreaking approach to solving the inverse scattering problem has been developed, utilizing a combination of deep learning and variational principles. In this study, a unified deep neural network was designed, integrating features from both classical optimization and optimization-based deep learning methods. By leveraging the strengths of these techniques, a unified neural network architecture was constructed that combines the incorporation of physical principles, invariances, and data. Compared to classical optimization methods, this new approach exhibits enhanced convergence speed, increased robustness to initialization, and higher accuracy. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that this new network can effectively learn to solve inverse scattering problems with varying material properties, without requiring explicit examples of the target material.

Reliability engineering utilizes accelerated degradation testing (ADT) to quickly assess highly reliable systems by exaggerating the effects of degradation, allowing for predictions about their reliability characteristics under normal conditions. One widely used method for analyzing ADT data is the model-based approach, which uses a specific reliability model to make predictions. This study introduces a new model-based inference method for ADT that incorporates information from multiple models to provide more accurate results. The method calculates the average of the mean estimates of individual models, along with an adjusted version that also considers the variance of the individual models, thereby improving the robustness of the model-based inference in ADT. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a simulated case study examining its accuracy under different conditions.

We investigate the connection between initial state fluctuations and triangular flow by examining the influence of eccentricity fluctuations on $v_3$. This is achieved by analyzing $v_3$ in relation to centrality and number of participants, as well as its dependence on initial time and geometry, within the context of a hydrodynamic model and event-by-event simulations. Our research reveals that the flow depends significantly on initial conditions and demonstrates that the initial time and geometry of the system play a crucial role in the magnitude of $v_3$. Furthermore, we identify an optimal centrality value at which $v_3$ reaches its maximum, in addition to highlighting the impact of fluctuations in initial conditions on initial time-dependent $v_3$ and illustrating its dependence on geometry.

We've obtained comprehensive observations of Interface Pulses (IPUs) from the combined data of STEREO-A, SOHO, and Wind spacecraft during the period of May 2009 to February 2017, encompassing multiple ICMEs observed by STERAE-A and SOHO. Utilizing these data, we've identified a total of 32 IPUs from these events and have calculated their properties. Our research revealed that ICMEs with IPUs exhibit a universal behavior of polytropic gas expansion, which is consistent with their thermodynamic conditions. Notably, this pattern holds true for all observed ICMEs, including those studied by this research and by other scientists, such as of the study by Russell et al. (2010). Our research also found that IPUs are closely related to magnetic reconnection, which is a process known to occur in solar wind CMEs. Based on this, we propose that IPUs are caused by magnetic reconnection occurring in the magnetic flux ropes of CMEs, specifically through a process known as reconnection at the U-shaped current sheet. Our research provides new insights into the physical processes governing ICMEs, which will be crucial for understanding their behavior, and has significant implications for space weather forecasting.

A long-standing question in Mobile Ad-Hoc Networks has been resolved, as it can now be shown that under the Random Waypoint Mobility Model, separation between node trajectories is possible with probability 1, using Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem, regardless of the specific randomization used.

The production of $K^+K^-$ pairs has been extensively studied by the KLOE collaboration at the DA$\Phi$3 facility, employing a sample of $1.7 \times 10^8$ $e^+e^-$ annihilation events at $\sqrt{s} = 1.02$ GeV. The investigation encompasses differential cross section measurements, transverse momentum distributions, and correlations between $K^+K^-$ pairs, alongside the effects of final state interactions on longitudinal momentum distributions. These studies are complemented by an analysis of the $K^+K^-$ mass spectrum, where the $f_0(980)$ resonance is observed to decay into a $K^+K^-$ pair, and the $f_0(980)$ and $\phi(1020)$ resonances are identified within the $K^+K^-$ mass spectrum. The experimental results are compared to the predictions of chiral perturbation theory, the $K\bar{K}$ vector meson model, and the hadron loop model.

The inertial masses for nuclear collective motion are calculated using the Green's function technique in the time-dependent Hartree-Fock theory to assess the sensitivity of these calculations to initial states and collective parameters. By comparing the microscopically calculated values with macroscopically estimated values from energy surface excitations, it is found that their sensitivity to initial states differs, with both sets exhibiting varying sensitivity.

A comprehensive and publicly accessible benchmark, known as the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC), has been developed to evaluate the capabilities of cutting-edge artificial intelligence algorithms in areas like healthcare diagnostics, autonomous driving, and smart homes. ARC consists of a large, diverse set of interactive tasks that test the ability of artificial intelligence systems to apply logical reasoning in real-world scenarios. We are introducing ARC as a benchmark for modern artificial intelligence systems, outlining a set of challenges and recommending guidelines for the design, evaluation, and implementation of advanced artificial intelligence systems. We also present a baseline evaluation using reinforcement learning algorithms, highlighting the opportunities and difficulties that come with developing artificial intelligence systems capable of solving ARC's complex tasks.

This study examines the mathematical model of scalar conservation laws with discontinuous flux functions, and our numerical approach utilizes a new type of stabilized, explicit methods on unstructured, simplicial meshes. We establish local error control near discontinuities in the flux for the first time by leveraging a fractional BV norm in a new class of well-balanced methods. Our findings are supported by numerical results showcasing second-order accuracy in the fractional BV norm for the solution and its flux, even in the presence of sharp discontinuities.

Measurements of branching fractions and the $B_{s}^{0}$ to $D_{s}^{\mp} K^{\pm}$ / $B_{s}^{0}$ to $D_{s}^{-} \pi^{+}$ ratio in $pp$ collisions at the LHCb detector are made in $1$ fb$^{-1}$ of data collected at a 7 TeV center-of-mass energy. The $B_{s}^{0}$ to $D_{s}^{\mp} K^{\pm}$ branching fraction relative to $B_{s}^{0}$ to $D_{s}^{-} \pi^{+}$ is found to be $2.9$ $\pm$ $0.2$ $\pm$ $0.2$ $\pm$ $0.2$ % or $B_{s}^{0}$ to $D_{s}^{+} K^{-}$ is $2.3$ $\pm$ $0.2$ $\pm$ $0.2$ $\pm$ $0.2$ % in agreement.

In this study, we investigated the optimal spectral efficiency in downlink systems that utilize massive MIMO and feature non-ideal phase alignment, specifically single-user (SU-MIMO) and multi-user (MU-MIMO) scenarios with a fixed pilot training period. To address the latter, we developed a novel subcarrier-based phase alignment technique that enables simultaneous data transmission with enhanced spectral efficiency. By introducing a subcarrier for phase alignment, we devised a phase estimation method to determine the phase offset for each BS antenna. The resulting phase-aided downlink training sequence (PATD) method exhibits superior performance over existing approaches. Furthermore, we proposed a novel MU-MIMO technique, involving the use of PATD, which incorporates a user scheduling strategy that considers channel rank and utilizes maximum-rank scheduling to optimize spectral efficiency.

A novel privacy model has been proposed, namely the shuffle model of differential privacy. It enhances traditional local privacy mechanisms by incorporating a shuffle mechanism, where users upload data without tracking individual submissions. The model relies on a central server performing a random shuffling of user inputs, which provides more effective data utilization compared to local privacy mechanisms. The application of this model in regression tasks has already shown promising results. This study presents a theoretical framework for semi-supervised learning within the shuffle model, demonstrating its ability to achieve superior performance for certain tasks. The shuffle model allows semi-supervised classification to achieve notable improvements, particularly in high-noise settings where the amount of labeled data is limited. The model also enables the achievement of semi-supervised classification error rates comparable to those of purely supervised learning methods with only half the amount of labeled data, thereby offering valuable insights into its potential applications.

A newly developed orthogonal time sequency multiplexing (OTSM) technique has shown promise as a single-carrier modulation method that outperforms OFDM in terms of spectrum efficiency. The paper first examines the basic working mechanism of single-carrier orthogonal sampling, followed by the derivation of an analytical expression for OTSM's probability density function, enabling a Gaussian approximation. Building upon this, an OTSM system with an iterative channel decoding is proposed, where the channel's impact is first factored out to simplify the decoding process, yielding improved performance by iterative decoding. Notably, the developed iterative decoder achieves comparable performance to that of OFDM systems with BPSK modulation over Rayleigh channels under a data transfer rate of 10 Mbps.

Let's denote the weight on a semigroup $S$ as $w$. The weighted harmonic algebra of $S$ is defined as the algebra consisting of $S$'s central functions that satisfy the $\mu$-harmonic condition, where $\mu$ represents a certain weighted measure of $u \circ u^{-1}$. The semigroup $S$ is said to possess the F-property if for any weighted measure $\mu$, it is true that for every $u \in S$, $u$ must be equivalent to $u^{-1}$ or the support of $\mu$ is a singleton set, effectively reducing to the case where $\mu$ is the Dirac measure. The F-property is established when $S$ is a group, and the F-property is also inherent in the regular subsemigroups of groups, but it is not inherent in the free semigroup. The F-property is studied in the context of certain classes of semigroups, specifically $T_{\kappa}$, $T_{\kappa}^{\ast}$, and $T_{\kappa}^{\circ}$. The investigation of the F-property is carried out in the context of regular subsemigroups, and the F-property is studied in the context of weighted harmonic algebras of $T_{\kappa}^{\ast}$ and $T_{\kappa}^{\circ}$.

The dynamic behavior of a molten metal melt pool under varying energy fluxes and thermal properties is examined through a set of non-dimensionalised, non-linear partial differential equations governing velocity and temperature. The study focuses on melt pool behavior under decreasing energy flux in a solid substrate. The influence of the Boussinesq approximation and its limitations are discussed, particularly on melt pool behavior in real-world applications. The study also investigates the effect of non-dimensionalised parameters on melt pool dynamics and concludes with an in-depth analysis of melt pool behavior under common welding conditions, including the transition from convection-dominated to diffusion-dominated regimes.

In the future 6G network, public transportation vehicles such as buses and trains are likely to incorporate wireless technology for radio communication and device recharging. By doing so, vehicles can provide an energy harvesting method for passengers, thus enhancing their usability and reducing waste. However, when vehicles and devices are in motion, it can be difficult to accurately position and align the recharging components, particularly when there are limited available spaces. In this context, we propose an innovative solution using a robotic recharging system, where a robotic device places the devices in the optimal position, allowing for efficient power harvesting from the vehicle's integrated energy harvesting infrastructure. Our proposed system is analyzed using a 3D simulation model, taking into account various factors, including different device shapes, robot designs, magnetic coupling, and vehicle movement scenarios with varying speeds. Our results show that the robotic device can successfully navigate and recharge devices at high speeds of up to 80 km/h in most cases, utilizing magnetic coupling and a certain amount of space.

Bistability is a common occurrence across various scientific disciplines, encompassing physical, biological, and engineering contexts. It is characterized by two stable states in a system, which can arise from either two distinct equilibrium values or two distinct periodic patterns. Our research focuses on understanding the origin of this phenomenon, particularly in systems driven by piecewise smooth periodic external forces. Through a dynamical systems approach, we identify the underlying conditions that give rise to bistability and derive a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for its occurrence. Furthermore, we develop a method to determine the locations of bistable structures within the parameter space, building upon the concept of Filippov subsystems. Ultimately, our framework is applied to two distinct types of bistable structures: equilibrium-value bistability and pattern bistability, and we demonstrate the practical utility of our results through numerical examples.

Our research involves analyzing the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a unified force field, at finite temperatures and varying baryonic densities. This investigation focuses on a model that incorporates the confinement hypothesis of QCD, specifically the nonlinear effective potential of MIT-Brazil bag-like quarks. We have calculated and graphically represented various thermodynamic parameters, including pressure, specific heat, entropy, and other relevant quantities, as functions of temperature and baryonic density, and compared them with those of unpolarized quark matter. We found that spin polarization leads to softer pressure and a less significant reduction in bag pressure at high densities, and that this difference becomes more pronounced at temperatures below 50 MeV. These results are relevant for understanding the properties of spin-polarized strange quark stars.

This study presents an in-depth examination of the key aspects associated with
audio-visual correlation learning. A comprehensive review is provided, highlighting
the primary goals, challenges, and evaluation metrics driving the advancement of
visual audio signal restoration. The findings are structured around three primary
goals - visual audio inference, audio generation from video, and general audio signal
restoration - and several subcategories. A detailed analysis of the used datasets,
network architectures, and metrics for measuring performance is also conducted.
The shortcomings of existing works and potential avenues for further research are
also discussed. It is anticipated that this review will provide a valuable resource for
new researchers entering this dynamic field.

A linear ordering problem involves selecting a optimal sequence from a set of n items, where the items are distinct and the selection order matters. Enumerating all possible sequences shows the complexity of this problem to be O(n!), making it unfeasible for large n. A more practical approach involves using heuristics to find good but not necessarily optimal solutions, and traditional methods typically require a high memory capacity to store all possible sequences. This paper presents a novel, high-performance solution that efficiently stores only one sequence at a time, and its source code is available on the repository at https://github.com/ChunYan-FangLin/Gap-Lop.

The Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase transition holds significant importance for understanding the transition to the normal state in low-dimensional superconductors. The complex phase diagram of cuprate superconductors, influenced by doping and temperature, poses a significant challenge to BKT transition studies in 2D materials. Our study focuses on the phase transition in underdoped YBa$_2$Cu$_4$O$_8$ (YBCO-124), a material exhibiting a 2D cuprate behavior, by analyzing the thermal response of Josephson coupling. Our findings indicate that the interlayer Josephson coupling in YBCO-124 exhibits a BKT transition, characterized by a critical temperature of 7.0 K. Our research contributes to the understanding of the transition towards the pseudogap phase in high-temperature superconductors, while also providing a new method for detecting BKT transitions in similar systems.

Temporal property graphs are advanced graph formats that incorporate in-depth temporal and semantic details, enabling the representation of complex objects and their associated attributes and relationships across multiple points in time. These graphs are particularly useful in areas such as digital health care, smart energy systems, and supply chain management, where the dynamic nature of entities and relationships plays a crucial role. This chapter provides an in-depth examination of temporal property graphs, including key concepts, characteristics, applications, advantages, strengths and weaknesses, and practical uses. We also cover the fundamental use cases, essential operations, and best practices for creating and interacting with temporal property graphs.

The unique properties of ultracold reactions create opportunities for in-depth
study and precise manipulation of molecular interactions, which is often
difficult to achieve in warmer environments. In addition to pure reactivity
studies, these reactions can also be utilized as a starting point to produce
molecular products with pre-determined quantum characteristics. To this end,
our experiments investigate the ultracold reactions $^{39}$K$^{39}$K + $^{39}$K$^{39}$K +
$^{39}$K $^{39}$K$^{39}$K and $^{39}$K $^{39}$K + HD, which have been
previously observed to be among the slowest chemical reactions. By employing
the Cold-Atom Reactions in Optical Lattices (CAL) technique, our experiments
not only reveal the precise timing of these reactions but also demonstrate the
effectiveness of this novel approach in fine-tuning the outcome of molecular
interactions.

We detail the enhanced software tools and the updated software infrastructure of the Swift/BAT hard X-ray survey data release 4, which offers a substantial enhancement in data analysis speed, accuracy and accessibility. This data release 4 includes a new, low-latency analysis capability that enables users to perform the principal components of the data analysis tools, thereby facilitating quick and preliminary research. We illustrate the Swift/BAT data release 4 usability through two distinct applications: the real-time detection of transient X-ray events and the automated classification of the BAT sky into active and inactive regions. The data analysis software and its design architecture are also discussed to promote transparency, accountability and reproducibility.

The phase diagram of the spin-1/2 J1-J2 XY model has been widely studied within the context of quantum many-body theories. However, recent numerical and experimental research has revealed a phase diagram differing from the previously accepted one. We confirm this revised phase diagram at zero temperature within the context of a classical spin model. The specific ratio of J2 to J1, particularly in the range of 0.5 to 0.75, determines whether the system is in the Néel, dimer, or cluster phase. Furthermore, in the limit of equal couplings, the Néel and dimer phases coexist in a specific region.

This research delves into the effects of global economic instability on trade balances. It employs a structural model to distinguish between persistent and fleeting economic shocks affecting major trading nations from 1970 to 2012, utilizing a recently updated trade dataset that accounts for the rise in trade transactions between specific countries. Typically, methods used to separate persistent from fleeting shocks require the homogeneity of shocks across different groups of countries. This study addresses this issue by estimating multiple sets of structural models, each focusing on a distinct group of countries chosen to meet this assumption. Each set of models is then utilized to calculate shock impacts, which are then aggregated to produce a unified metric measuring the effects of global economic instability on trade balances. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that separating pervasive and nonpervasive shocks is essential for determining the most likely causes of trade imbalances among developed countries since 2008.

A noncommutative gauge theory in four dimensions involves an additional commutative coordinate with a noncommuting spatial coordinate, and by performing a coordinate transformation along with a gauge transformation, it can be transformed into a conventional gauge theory in four dimensions. This research provides a generalization of the above idea to $2\times 2$ matrices used as additional coordinates, and defines a class of the Lie algebra $E(2,2)$ that can be used to generate these transformations for various elements of the algebra. The research involves the construction of the Lie algebra $E(2,2)$ through both the Poisson and Darboux bases, and the construction of the Lie algebra $E(2,2)$ with the help of the Lie algebra $E(2,2)$, which is referred to as the adjoint algebra, and the explicit transformation of the noncommutative gauge field to the conventional field is obtained.

This research investigates a coherent filtering problem within the context of quantum mechanics on an infinite timeline. Our objective is to find the optimal control strategy that minimizes the infinite-time cost expressed as the expectation value of an exponentially-weighted Hamiltonian for a two-level quantum system interacting with coherent light. By solving the finite-dimensional time-optimal control problem using Pontryagin's minimum principle, we develop a family of filters that serve as the quantum equivalent of the Kalman filter. This filter enables real-time estimation of unknown variables within quantum communication systems, potentially reaching optimal efficiency.

A person's perception of time (POTP) is closely linked to their emotional state and response to stress, offering a measurable indicator of their mental health. Our study develops an experiment-based approach to assess POTP and designs a machine learning challenge to analyze the time-related implications of the experiment's results. We provide insights into our findings and propose future research avenues related to time analysis.

This research investigation aims to examine how quickly and accurately professionals make decisions, specifically during a controlled chess session where they are forced to choose between accepting or rejecting an offer in a unique endgame scenario. The study adds to the decision-making research literature by combining a laboratory setting with a simulation environment, allowing for the analysis of speed and quality separately. The outcomes of this study were compared with a previous study by Corgnet et al. using a similar setup but without the simulation element. The outcomes of this study were also compared to a previous study where speed and quality were not separated. The study found that professionals were able to make decisions as quickly as in the Corgnet study, but that their performance was less accurate, resulting in losses in the simulated game. The study's results also suggest that professionals were able to make faster decisions without sacrificing accuracy, but that some level of inaccuracy was inherent in their decision-making process. The study's findings indicate that professionals were able to adapt to the simulated game, but that they struggled to replicate their typical level of performance in this new setting.

Previous research has highlighted the disparities in how machine learning fairness definitions and legal concepts regarding discrimination treat individuals differently. To further explore this, a study was conducted that compares the mathematical and legal approaches to identifying members of groups protected by anti-discrimination laws. The analysis focuses on two key differences: the use of "protected attributes" and the criteria for determining membership in protected groups. The results indicate that the mathematical approach often produces results that deviate from the legal understanding of these concepts.

Two significant types of neutrino mass distinctions have been found in recent studies, including the distinction between squared mass differences and the hierarchy of squared masses. Researchers are now exploring a novel difference, referred to as the deviation from unitarity in lepton mixing matrices, which can be explored through experiments such as the DUNE and JUNO projects. The discussion also touches on recent advances in understanding unitarity from a theoretical perspective.

We have studied $^{5}_{\Lambda}$He, $^{5}_{\Sigma}$He, and $^{5}_{\Lambda}$H using the effective field theory baryon-baryon interaction N3LO. Our calculations took into account the quantum electrodynamics radiative corrections for the emission of a single neutron from $\Lambda$- $^{4}$He and $\Sigma$- $^{4}$He. Two QCD-inspired BB interactions, N3LOUR and N3LOMP, were used, and we found that their use led to different $\Lambda N$ separation energies. Our results for the $\Lambda N$ scalar pole mass show a significant variation among these two interactions, and we found this to have a considerable effect on the calculation of emission probabilities. Our findings for the $\Sigma N$ scalar pole mass revealed a more limited agreement among the two QCD-inspired BB interactions, especially when it comes to the emission of a neutron from $\Sigma$- $^{4}$He.

Social media platforms have become essential for both personal and professional interactions, but they raise significant concerns over user privacy. The increasing number of users on these platforms has led to a surge in data breaches and cyber-attacks. This research aims to enhance user privacy on social media by leveraging a proxy server system. The proposed solution involves installing a proxy server to mitigate the risk of data breaches and cyber-attacks on social media platforms. Users can access their account by connecting to the proxy server instead of the actual website. To test the effectiveness of this approach, a study compared the response time of Facebook when accessing it through the proposed proxy server system with direct access to the website. The results showed that using the proxy server had a negligible impact on response time. Consequently, users can rely on the proxy server to maintain their privacy when using social media without noticeable delays.

Consider a neutral coalescent process in a continuously changing environment with a positive rate function $R(t)$ and let $T$ be the time at which three lineages merge. This paper investigates the properties and behavior of $T$ under the condition that R follows a specific type of stochastic process. We focus on a class of rate functions with a particular distribution. We derive a set of general theorems describing the distribution of $T$ in various scenarios and then apply them to specific cases, including a normal distribution for $R(t)$. We use a particular approach to derive explicit formulas for the distribution of $T$ in these cases and verify the results through simulation experiments.

We investigate a hard core model on the Cayley tree, specified by positive symmetric matrices of infinite order. The model's primary phase can be described by a system of equations involving the matrices' eigenvalues, which characterizes the periodic Gibbs measures. Additionally, we derive explicit formulas for the characteristics of periodic measures in this system.

The LAMOST survey, a massive and in-depth investigation of the Milky Way and surrounding galaxies, employs a dual approach. This involves using photometric and spectroscopic methods to gather data. While the photometric method excels at measuring large-scale structures and has been highly successful, its reliance on color selection techniques poses limitations. Conversely, spectroscopic methods provide crucial information on the structure and dynamics of galaxies by analyzing stellar spectra, yet their scope is often restricted by their observational nature. To leverage the strengths of both methods, this study presents a novel approach - combining photometric and spectroscopic data to create a comprehensive and uniform sample of galaxies. This integrated dataset, known as the LAMOST Survey Sample (LSS), consists of 1,300 galaxies with specific characteristics and covers a broad range of redshift values. By utilizing the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey mock galaxy catalog, the LSS was constructed and validated through a thorough comparison with the MUSE-Hi galaxy catalog. This study further demonstrates the efficacy of the LSS through a series of tests, including the examination of redshift evolution and the correlation between stellar mass and velocity dispersion.

To investigate the unknown nuclear charge radii of the rare isotopes Tl-201, Tl-203, and Tl-205, we conducted precise isotope-shift measurements of the Tl-205 nucleus for comparison. We used a fast atomic beam technique coupled with a double Penning-tron ionization chamber to obtain accurate results. By comparing the isotope shifts of the Tl-205 nucleus with those of the Tl-201 and Tl-203 nuclei whose radii are known, we were able to determine the nuclear charge radii of Tl-201, 203, and 205. These results reveal a distinct separation of the Tl isotopes, with their nuclear charge radii following a trend of increasing size as the isotopic mass increases.

In the field of quantum information theory, researchers define graph states as specific quantum states represented by graphs, characterized by their entanglement patterns. Graph states are distinguished by a set of independent logical qubits. Our study develops a new method to generate an arbitrary graph state using a more basic quantum resource, namely a single-photon source, and a device capable of measuring light frequencies. We reevaluate the process of creating a graph state using a more reliable single-photon source, and compare it to the previously used two-photon source approach, revealing that single-photon sources offer improved performance and reliability. Our research further demonstrates the feasibility of using optical frequency and time domains to represent graph states, and that detecting graph states is possible through simple spectroscopic measurements.

Hall's Theorem provides a crucial condition for a family of sets to have a transversal: the cardinality of each set must be greater than or equal to the count of matching elements from each set in that family. This paper builds upon the concept of partially ordered sets, where sets are categorized in descending order based on their element count. It focuses on transversals in families of these partially ordered sets, introducing a modified version of Hall's Theorem that applies to such families. This revised theorem asserts that for each subset within the family of partially ordered sets, the count of matching elements from each subset in that family must be greater than or equal to the count of subsets in that subset.

This research examines video encoding and video storage requirements for cloud services. We've developed a framework for analyzing video content based on its spatial and temporal resolution, employing two parameters to describe the probability distributions of these characteristics for each second of a video. This framework uses the proposed parameters to predict video encoding duration and storage needs for a specific cloud provider, allowing us to evaluate the performance of cloud services in relation to video encoding and storage demands, taking into account the available computing resources of the cloud. We've also developed a method for determining the optimal virtual machine configuration for video encoding operations.

We develop a comprehensive approach to determine and analyze probabilities in random low-density triangle structures, focusing on specific instances where the density decreases substantially. In the range where triangle density is relatively high ($t$ between $t_0$ and $t_1$, with $t_0$ and $t_1$ defined by the given mathematical expressions), we show that the likelihood of a random graph with a triangle density of $t$ decreasing by a factor of $t^3$ is approximately $t^3$ (with an error margin of $t^5$) when the number of graph vertices ($n$) is on the order of $1/t$ and increasing.

This paper investigates the ground state of the renormalized Gross-Pitaevskii equation, specifically when it is heavily imbalanced with only a single component. The research shows that, in a situation where there is an external harmonic potential, the state will collapse towards a single point for an extremely large non-linearity level and will exist as separate entities for a non-extreme non-linearity level. In both scenarios, the study provides an accurate representation of the ground state using an error margin measured by a $H^{-1}$-norm of less than $C\sqrt{\varepsilon}$, with 'C' representing a constant value.

A specific pre-testing design called the adaptive calibration (AC) procedure is developed to regulate its control at a specific alpha level despite varying effect sizes in the alternative hypothesis space. This adaptation method utilizes the alpha level by allocating it among regions based on the distribution of test statistics under the null and alternative hypotheses. The allocation of alpha values to different regions is adjusted to maintain the overall alpha level while maximizing the power of the test for smaller effect sizes within the alternative hypothesis space. The AC procedure is applied to the frequentist inference of the mean of a normal distribution with unknown variance. The AC procedure is also evaluated using a Bayesian hierarchical model for normal responses with unknown mean and variance, and a modified version called posterior intervals (PI) which uses the posterior median of the posterior probability density of the null hypothesis based on the Bayes factor. The Bayes factor is calculated using the Littell-Barton likelihood ratio test statistic. The Bayes PI procedure is shown to be more powerful than the frequentist AC procedure for small effect sizes within the alternative hypothesis space, while controlling its false positive rate within the specified alpha level.

We introduce a novel method for hybrid rendering, an approach ideal for self-contained extended reality devices that integrate external light capture and display technologies. The method enables the simultaneous rendering of real-world and virtual components, allowing for seamless interaction with real-world environments. The method consists of three key stages: real-world environment analysis, virtual object rendering, and combined rendering. By leveraging external light capture, this method can be implemented entirely on the device's CPU, eliminating the need for a powerful GPU. Furthermore, this method can be adapted to support volumetric extensions and dynamic environments, making it suitable for complex scenarios.

Comparing annotations from various sources in music is crucial for timely research applications, but the reliability of this comparison is contingent upon the consistency in annotation timing between human annotators. This paper investigates the discrepancies in annotation timing between human annotators and machines, specifically highlighting variations found in a study involving five annotators with over 15 months of consecutive annotations and examining the differences between annotations made by these individuals. The results reveal that the level of inaccuracy is not consistent across all parameters and that the deviations between human annotators themselves can be substantial, warranting greater consideration in comparative studies and the development of machine learning algorithms.

In-band full-duplex technology enables high efficiency by doubling the cell capacity without increasing bandwidth, yet it's hindered by self-interference. Our study focuses on this challenge by proposing an approach to mitigate it within a multi-antenna setup. We develop a linear pre-coder to eliminate self-interference effectively, identify its inherent limitations, and establish the optimal solution. Additionally, we introduce a power allocation method to minimize the overall interference level. It's surprising to note that in this two-way communication, the transmitter's received signal can sometimes be a better solution for eliminating interference than the traditionally used receiver signal.

We investigate the formation of pattern networks within colloidal droplets and their final solid forms, focusing on how pressure-driven water evaporation creates intricate designs. As the droplet dries out, the surface undergoes a series of buckling events due to stress, resulting in spiky features and subsequent relaxation into stable pattern networks connected by thin ridges. Our study reveals that these networks are comprised of two distinct types of buckled lines: those that arise from regular patterns at the base of the droplet and those that do not, emerging from areas with high curvature. By applying principles from theories of fracture and materials with negative stiffness, we explain the development of these networks and the unique, interconnected pattern elements they contain.

Protoplanetary disks' CO and H2 emissions have distinct patterns within their outer regions. CO emission appears at greater distances from the central star compared to H2 emission. This discrepancy is attributed to the differing formation mechanisms of these molecules. CO is expected to form in areas where the gas temperature is too low for standard chemical reactions to occur. This temperature threshold is consistent with the lowest temperatures where CO is observed in these disks. This discovery supports the gas-dust separation model for CO evolution. This model suggests that CO desorption is restricted to ice-grain interfaces and does not occur in areas where CO is thermally evaporated. This model is consistent with observations of CO spatial distribution in these disks.

This paper introduces an innovative deep learning approach to enhance millimeter wave positioning by leveraging the unique characteristics of the human body to pinpoint objects. The proposed technique estimates the space-time channel response vector of a user device based on measurements from an access point and utilizes a trained deep learning model to calculate the absolute position of the user. To model the human body's effect on millimeter wave signals, we rely on Monte Carlo simulations that calculate the space-time channel response vector as the weighted sum of individual body parts' contributions. The trained deep learning model combines these simulations with time and frequency domain measurements of the user device to determine its absolute position, showing that it significantly improves the user's location relative to conventional methods that ignore human interference or assume a single reflecting surface.

In a vacuum, we produced particles with orbital angular momenta by irradiating a quantum target with circularly polarized light within a uniform magnetic field. Our theoretical framework examined the nonlinear optical process for x-ray generation, specifically investigating the production of elliptically polarized X-ray photons with specific orbital angular momenta when a hydrogen atom is in a uniform magnetic field. Our calculations were based on the sum-over-states method, employing a variational solution to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for the electron's wave function, and taking into account the atomic target's nuclear Coulomb potential.

This research paper examines the issue of strategically locating electric vehicle charging stations to maximize customer satisfaction and reduce energy loss through the public grid. A novel approach using a mixed-integer linear programming model, taking into account the interactions between EV users and charging stations, is proposed to optimize the charging schedule. A hybrid algorithm is further developed to efficiently handle large-scale problems. Specifically, a decomposition method separates the problem into smaller, independent charging tasks, which are then solved using the algorithm, and a local search procedure is applied to improve the quality of the optimal solution. Through various numerical experiments, the efficacy of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated, and its practical implications are discussed.

In two-stage regression designs, researchers use optimization methods to find the optimal value of a running variable that minimizes the variance of a treatment effect estimator in a specific design. Optimal designs can be classified into various types based on the type of estimator used, the method of optimization employed, and the level of optimization assurance. This study focuses on optimizing two-stage regression designs with restricted treatment assignments, a mean cost function, and a non-differentiable objective function resulting from the use of the generalized propensity score. By utilizing a stochastic gradient descent method, the researchers propose a locally optimal solution that is capable of handling non-smooth objectives and high-dimensional designs. The proposed method is evaluated through a simulation study to assess its performance in small sample sizes.

Using superconformal techniques, we develop a formula for three-point functions involving multiple protected operators in SU(N) N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Our results align when considering two identical couplings in the situation described by Arkani-Hamed, Polchinski, Silverstein, and Sundrum. Moreover, applying superconformal methods for three-point functions can be adapted to determine the cross-sections of four-point amplitudes in the corresponding super Amplitudes context.

Engaging children in creative and interactive activities through play and exploration is essential for their cognitive development, particularly in areas like language acquisition and problem-solving. Recent studies have highlighted the benefits of technology-assisted playful learning experiences for children, specifically in developing essential 21st-century skills. Building on these findings, this study investigates the practical applications of AI-enhanced playful learning for young children (2-7 years old) and explores the effectiveness of ML-driven activities in fostering creativity, adaptability, and critical thinking skills. Furthermore, the study aims to identify the characteristics of efficient PL environments that support children's social, emotional, and physical growth.

Lifelong reinforcement learning (LRL) is a complex field where reinforcement learning (RL) and continual learning (CL) meet, and its unique challenges have led to the development of distinct methodologies. Current studies in LRL either focus on adapting RL within changing environments or making RL more like CL by maintaining past knowledge through a single, unified approach. To address the limitations of these one-size-fits-all methods, we propose a new framework that differentiates between RL and CL, allowing them to coexist to optimize policy adaptation in LRL. Our framework integrates CL to aid RL in adapting to changing tasks and maintains the past knowledge of RL. We also introduce the concept of knowledge transfer efficiency (KTE) to gauge the effectiveness of transferring learned knowledge from previous tasks to new ones. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in LRL, especially in scenarios with limited training data.

To advance quantum computing, controlling multiple degrees of freedom is crucial to fully harness quantum technology's potential. Our study showcases this capability by integrating a single photon with high-order states in micro-ring resonators that can store and process quantum bits using a single type II wavelength dual-mode resonator. By manipulating and varying the photon's frequency, we demonstrate precise control over the optical interactions, allowing us to switch between single-photon and two-photon interactions at will. This innovation has the potential to significantly enhance the design of quantum processors incorporating non-linear optical processes, their optimization, and experimental implementation.

The study of nanoscale physics has led to the development of highly sensitive tools for genetic research, including DNA analysis. A thorough examination of a DNA molecule's unique properties is crucial for comprehending its behavior in electronic devices. A DNA molecule's non-linear electrical properties make it challenging to model its behavior, thus limiting its application as a switching element in logic gates. A study on a DNA hairpin with a specific mismatched base pair, (GA), has been conducted to investigate its electrical characteristics. The results show that the mismatched base pair significantly increases the electrical current compared to a DNA molecule with a perfectly paired (TA) base pair, particularly when a small voltage is applied. The study suggests that the mismatched base pair, specifically the (GA) pair, can function as a sensitive electrical detector, with an estimated limit of detection of 0.1 femtoamps at 0.01 volts. The study's findings contribute to the understanding of DNA's electrical properties and the development of devices that can utilize DNA's inherent properties.

The registration problem involves aligning multiple views of a scene, and despite various solutions proposed over the years, there is a persistent issue with existing methods. These methods prioritize speed and efficiency but compromise on accuracy and robustness, failing to adapt to diverse applications. The key limitation lies in the narrow definition of the registration problem, causing usability to be constrained by factors such as scale, correspondence, and convergence. We propose redefining the problem, incorporating a comprehensive evaluation of the desired use case. This new perspective enables the incorporation of auxiliary variables and the incorporation of additional robustness measures. By treating this as an ill-posed problem, we can introduce new variables to make it solvable. Our method, called the Robustly Constrained Algorithm, has been tested on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets and has shown superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

Our research explores the magnetic characteristics of Tb3RuO7, an oxygen-deficient striped strip perovskite where Ru is present in two distinct states. Through the use of neutron powder diffraction, we observed that, except for low-temperature conditions, the magnetic configurations of Ru1 and Ru2 are parallel and exhibit the same degree of order. Below 15 Kelvin, the Ru1 moments undergo an ordered state while Ru2 remains disordered in time, with its disordered state being influenced by Ru1. As a result, the magnetic ordering in Tb3RuO7 is unique, featuring a complex interplay between the moments' alignment.

This research offers a general framework for the study of constrained mathematical programming problems in locally convex spaces. By leveraging connections to the theory of optimization within Banach spaces, we establish key criteria for Nonsmooth and Gaivoronsky--Kikinzon results, which may be applied to specific types of problems with specific spatial properties, specifically those with a Fr\'{e}chet space. Additionally, we examine specific scenarios related to generalized Nash equilibrium and reveal novel insights under mild assumptions. Furthermore, we investigate the utility of our research in the context of European Union emissions trading scheme with respect to carbon footprint reductions.

We explore IIA solutions featuring D6-over-D4 configurations, particularly in cases involving O1-planes with associated D6/ D4 geometries. These solutions are characterized by specific solutions to the M5/BPS equations. These solutions exhibit supersymmetry for odd dimensions and also satisfy the topological couplings. We have found solutions in IIA gauge groups of the form U(N) x U(1-N) for various gauge coupling constants. These solutions are connected to previously derived M5/BPS solutions in string theory. We have also discovered novel solutions in gauge group U(1-N) featuring an O3-plane.

In a strongly-coupled gauge theory that undergoes a thermal phase transition, we examine how phase domains collide. Our study employs an effective field theory that models the collision by virtue of a hierarchy in its hierarchy of large and small length scales. At low collision velocities, phase domains merge into a single, connected entity. However, at high velocities, they shatter into separate regions. An intermediate scenario where the domain walls momentarily close to infinity is also considered.
