This finding allows for the development of a polynomial-time heuristic, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through both simulated and real-world data experiments.

In the field of survival analysis for time-to-event data, flexible and interpretable models are highly valued, yet the majority of parametric hazard models are poorly interpretable. To address this, a novel approach is introduced, utilizing the logistic regression framework to estimate parametric hazard functions and leveraging the resulting interpretable coefficients to represent time-dependent hazard rates. To enhance model performance, an auxiliary variable is incorporated to enhance the learning process. To validate this method, a simulation study is conducted, and a case study is used to demonstrate its effectiveness.

In the Standard Model of modern particle physics, strong electromagnetic forces are combined into the electroweak force by mixing with QCD.  The development of a three-loop all-order electroweak correction is currently a highly challenging project in modern theoretical physics, however various two-loop corrections have been computed for key processes such as W-pair production, Higgs boson decay, and top quark pair production, with results being compared with experimental data at the Large Hadron Collider.  This paper will review the current state of two-loop electroweak corrections, highlighting the key methods and tools used in their computation, particularly the two-loop electroweak mixing relations, with attention to algebraic, numerical, and computational challenges encountered during this process.  The discussion will also cover the application of these techniques to related areas, including three-loop BSM calculations, NNLL-resummation, and high-precision QCD calculations, with a focus on their impact and potential for future predictions in new physics searches.

In recent years, high-performance object stores have become increasingly popular in the HPC community as an alternative to traditional file systems for storing large datasets. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of current trends and needs within the field of high-performance computing (HPC) storage, with a focus on the capabilities and potential future developments of these object stores. Furthermore, we explore the current state of prominent open-source and commercial object stores, including their design features, scalability, performance, and availability.

This study examines the long-term allocation of a network of electric vehicle charging facilities that offer accommodation, convenience, and associated costs for users. To enhance user satisfaction, the facility owner offers a free initial charge for users who become regular customers. However, this approach increases operational costs and hampers resource utilization. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that integrates charging station operation with user satisfaction and reduced operational costs. We model the problem as a dynamic game where the facility owner and users make sequential decisions to maximize their benefits. By utilizing the Nash equilibrium framework, we derive an optimal policy that ensures no other policy results in a higher utility for the facility owner or users. We also provide a low-complexity approximation that is easy to implement without requiring a precise understanding of user behavior. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches in reducing operational costs while maintaining acceptable levels of user satisfaction.

We prove the existence of Euclidean and Hermitian linear complementary dual (LCD) codes with different parameters within finite fields. We also develop a method for generating Hermitian LCD codes from binary Hermitian LCD codes and apply this approach to create new Hermitian LCD codes of length $q^3+q^2$ with the best known parameters for several prime powers $q$.

Recent advancements in classical perturbation theory for general relativity involve loop integrals, which can be simplified by converting their multi-dimensional integrands into a 2-dimensional contour problem using Borel transformation. This process transforms the integral convergence issue into a contour definition in the complex plane. This approach is applied to the initial one-loop scattering of scalar, spinor, and vector particles within the context of Einstein-Hilbert gravity.

To find out if it's possible to generate zero-carbon electricity in the US through solar power alone, we used two different models. One of them considered only solar power from open spaces and the other included solar power from existing rooftops. The results showed that 78 to 85% of the solar power needed to generate zero-carbon electricity in the US could be produced using these sources. However, generating zero-cars and heat would still require other energy sources. The study also found that 78% of the solar power needed to produce zero-carbon electricity could be produced from open spaces, and 76% from existing rooftops.

We outline a methodological framework that supports the design, analysis, and validation of of vaccine trials characterized by complex primary endpoints. This framework emphasizes the necessity of defining estimands prior to the study, as well as identifying suitable statistical analyses and determining the underlying model structure to ensure estimand validity. Furthermore, we provide guidance on developing confidence intervals for estimands in the presence of missing data or structural model shortcomings.

Network spectrum analysis is a crucial area of research, focusing on characterizing how a network's structure impacts its various parameters. This study contributes to the understanding of networks by introducing a new approach to establish interconnections between spectral, topological, and entropy measures of networks. The proposed method is applied to directed and undirected graphs, providing novel findings that complement existing research in the field. The study examines the adjacency matrix and normalized Laplacian of these networks to derive new results regarding their spectral properties, and establishes sharp, algebraically inspired bounds for the smallest eigenvalue of directed graphs. Furthermore, we derive Laplacian-based measures for entropy and investigate their relationships with network size and order.

In a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit problem, we study an n-armed bandit scenario with a decision maker who possesses d additional features for each arm and receives a d-dimensional context for each reward before observing it. Given that communication is limited to a binary system, the decision maker must communicate the d-dimensional context to a central server that manages a joint policy across all features for each arm. Our research focuses on a centralized version of this problem that utilizes a binary tree structure, enabling the development of a new algorithm that achieves sublinear regret with high probability. Our algorithm, which requires a binary system, uses a fixed amount of space that scales with the number of arms and features but not the time horizon, enables the centralized version to achieve the first optimal results for contextual linear bandits with a binary communication system. Specifically, it can achieve an optimal time horizon of $\Tilde{O}(d \sqrt(En \log(1/\beta)))$ bits of communication and a sublinear regret with high probability of $\Oo(\sqrt(dEn \log(1/\beta)))$ for any given confidence parameter $\beta$ while matching existing optimal results for a centralized version without any limitations on the communication system.

The healthcare industry is rapidly adopting machine learning technologies, with applications in both clinical and non-clinical contexts. However, generating large datasets for training and validating machine learning models is a significant challenge, particularly in healthcare. An alternative solution is the creation of synthetic data that accurately mimics real-world scenarios, allowing for the implementation of machine learning models. In this study, we introduce a novel synthetic healthcare data generation method that utilizes tabular data. By incorporating a conditional variational autoencoder and a Residual Generative Adversarial Network, our approach effectively combines both the efficiency of generating data and the preservation of medical data integrity. Our method was evaluated through a series of quantitative and qualitative tests, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce real-world data and successfully identify patients based on recovered information. Our approach is open-sourced and available for public use, offering researchers a scalable and data-efficient solution for healthcare applications.

The initial measurement of the D0 meson decaying into K+ K- π- and π+ π- is presented, with the D0 being produced from e+ e- annihilation. The data, gathered by the BESIII detector, amount to 5.92 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity. The D0 meson decays are isolated with high accuracy using a fit function that separates the D0 signal from the background using specific characteristics of the D0 and its decay products. The branching fractions of the D0 decays are measured as follows: Fr = (4.46 ± 0.55 ± 0.39) × 10^-3 for the K+ K- π- decay, and Fr = (2.50 ± 0.78 ± 0.20) × 10^-3 for the π+ π- decay. The first uncertainty is statistical, while the second is due to systematic uncertainty.

A new metric, the Schatz, has been created to measure the innovation and disruptiveness of recent research. Unlike previous metrics, Schatz relies on a minimal set of requirements, making it applicable to a wide range of scientific studies. In a comprehensive examination, Schatz was compared to 10 existing bibliometric metrics on their capacity to distinguish innovative research. Our analysis involved evaluating the performance of these metrics on data from the US patent registry and combining them with Schatz. Our results showed that Schaz has significant value as a novel metric for measuring innovation. It is highly adaptable, requires minimal assumptions, and can be applied to a wide range of scientific fields. Furthermore, Schaz is highly effective in identifying recent breakthroughs and has the potential to be used as a tool for predicting future breakthroughs.

We have successfully achieved spatiotemporal pulse shaping of a 4.5 ps pulse from an Er:Yb:KGd(WO4)2 crystal, by introducing a brief stencil pulse with a duration of approximately 1 ps. This enabling technique provides a crucial step towards applying the fine structure constant and performing precise spectroscopic analyses on individual atoms. As proof of concept, we applied our method to modify the spatial and temporal profile of a laser, and produced a tailored pulse with a unique controllable shape and duration, ranging from 1 ps to 4.5 ps.

The primary objective of the RoboCup competition is to create a robotics team capable of winning against human opponents in a specific game, with the "Open RoboCup Simulator" (ORCS) providing a challenging environment for its participants. Focusing on "RoboCup 2020 - SafetyManeuver," this research aims to develop a fully autonomous safety-maneuvering robot with the assistance of a high-level decision-making approach and a low-level learning control method. By combining a deep reinforcement learning algorithm with a specific neural network architecture, our work successfully simulated a virtual simulator and secured a first-place finish in the competition.

Recent advancements in cross-domain recommendation have been largely limited to traditional methods that rely on shared machines and similar user groups. This limitation hinders the ability to transfer knowledge between domains, thus minimizing the benefits of cross-domain recommendation. To address this issue, we introduce a novel dual learning model that enables knowledge sharing between the source and target domains without requiring a shared platform. This model leverages both source and target views into a single latent space and incorporates a view-invariant regularizer to enhance performance. Additionally, we incorporate a domain memory-based knowledge transfer mechanism to distill and refine transferred knowledge. Experimental results demonstrate the superior efficacy of our proposed method compared to existing cross-domain recommendation approaches.

We investigate the duality between first-order logic and finite distributed systems, specifically through the use of distributed automata, for infinite graphs. We demonstrate that for finite, directed graphs, first-order logic has an equivalent in a certain type of asynchronous machine, known as asynchronous distributed automata, leading to an established correspondence between the two. Furthermore, this logic also equates to local first-order three-colorable graph logic, providing a broader understanding of the connection between logic and finite systems. We also establish that, for infinite, undirected graphs, first-order logic has an equivalent in a certain type of asynchronous distributed system, with certain restrictions in place, specifically symmetry and finite range of input.

A simplified two-dimensional fluid model is developed by introducing two- and three-body interactions, enabling a comparison with the corresponding three-dimensional fluid model. By integrating the structure factor and virial decomposition, the equation of state for the two-dimensional fluid is derived. Using the sound velocity and specific heat, the heat conductivity coefficient is determined. Calculations show that the heat conductivity coefficient matches the three-dimensional value when the two-dimensional fluid model is made equivalent to its three-dimensional counterpart. Our findings are extended to two-dimensional hard-sphere fluids using Monte Carlo simulations, which confirm that the equation of state and heat conductivity coefficient obtained from our simplified model are accurate for weak and moderate interaction strengths. However, for stronger interactions, our model underpredicts the equation of state and heat conductivity coefficient, necessitating the inclusion of three-body interactions.

We investigate the problem of finding a finitely generated subgroup to which a given data vector belongs, with components defined by a real-valued function. Our findings indicate that the data vector can join subsets of finitely generated subgroups if and only if it has a finite section of non-negative elements. This condition is also applicable when the data vector features reversible elements. A positive result is derived for the scenario where the data vector consists of integer components. Additionally, a proof demonstrates that the direct sum of finitely generated subgroups is equivalent to the direct sum of subsets of finitely generated subgroups.

A specific challenge in radiographic imaging involves minimizing the time of X-ray exposure during procedures like coronary angiography. To address this issue, researchers have developed a dynamic exposure reduction method. By adjusting exposure level according to the local image intensity, this dynamic approach aims to utilize the fullest portion of the detector's dynamic range in the acquired image. In this study, a novel real-time exposure control system was designed and integrated with the CARe challenge framework. To facilitate efficient testing of this algorithm, a simplified simulated workflow was developed. The simplified workflow allows for dynamic algorithm testing on the reconstructed, but X-ray exposure-adjusted, images. To further optimize this dynamic approach, researchers explored two specific adjustments to the workflow: adapting exposure based on frames and adjusting exposure per projection. The feasibility of this dynamic approach was successfully demonstrated in a preliminary test on the CARe challenge dataset.

The massive electron-positron collisions at the Future Circular Collider's enhanced low-energy centre of mass (1.5 TeV) will greatly benefit research into heavy-flavour physics, particularly by providing much higher statistics and enhanced precision than the current Belle II experiment. The enhanced statistics at FCC-ee will enable more precise measurements of heavy-flavour mass spectra, allowing for more accurate tests of theoretical models describing hadronization. The FCC-ee will also enable the heavy-flavour sector to test theories of electroweak symmetry breaking and new physics, through the measurement of heavy-flavour production in the low and high mass regimes.

The U(1)_{L_	e-a} model, a Z_2 symmetry that connects lepton family indices and family flavors, naturally breaks lepton flavor universality and offers a theoretical framework for neutrino mass generation through tri-linear effective interactions and coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering. This model's predictions for CEνNS are calculated based on its symmetry structure, and using the current linear response function from Burman et al., we find that for specific coupling values, a U_e-a coupling of around 10^-6 to 10^-4 and an U_μ-a coupling of around 10^-5, could enhance the CEνNS cross section to levels of X-Y orders of magnitude for both 232Th and 208Pb targets, respectively, within the current and near-future limits of sensitivity.

A new class of stars, known as hyper-velocity stars, moves rapidly and their origins are thought to stem from being dislodged from their star systems through interactions with supermassive black holes. Theorized to be the precursors to binary black hole formations, their study holds significant implications. The discovery of a new hyper-velocity star within the globular cluster 47 Tucanae, identified as V106, with a velocity of 443 km/s and a likely age of 13 billion years, presents a unique opportunity to observe the distribution of stars within a stable, densely packed system. The observation of V106 suggests that it likely resides in a previously uncharted region of space, with a potential distance of 0.3 parsecs from the center of 47 Tucanae, with a velocity consistent with both past ejections and future orbits. The study of V106's trajectory reveals that it may be the first recorded hyper-velocity star within a star system of this nature, with a potential future observation window that may reveal more of its path.

Multiplicative stochastic differential equations are solved under the framework of the Girsanov theorem within the context of the Banach space valued stochastic Cauchy problem. Conditions for the existence of probabilistically weak solutions, as well as the convergence of the corresponding discrete time approximations, are established. Additionally, a discussion of the long-term behavior of the one-dimensional Brownian motion-driven multiplicative stochastic differential equation is presented when it is formulated within the context of the space of continuous functions and the condition $\alpha\in(0,1]$, with $\alpha$ representing the fractional derivative exponent in the KGB martingale type multiplicative equation.

In $\bb V$ with a Woodin cardinal $\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is greater than $\omega_2$, $\NS_{\omega_1}$ is not definable by any $\Sigma_1$ formula, yet it becomes definable when $\kappa$ is replaced with $\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is some $\Sigma_1$-definable regular cardinal that is less than $\kappa$.

The goal of natural language processing is often misunderstood, leading to confusion between comprehending messages and merely recognizing their characteristics. Current approaches to NLP either focus solely on task outcomes or use objectives that are designed to avoid specific errors. In contrast, we propose an alternative method where the objective of analysis is systematically determined in relation to a particular task. This approach is illustrated through a case study in which a pre-trained transformer model is trained to classify sentiment by aligning its predictions with task-specific targets, thereby optimizing its performance on the target task. Furthermore, we present an extension to this method, which enables the creation of objective functions tailored to distinct NLP tasks without requiring task-specific training data. This enhanced method is applied to three diverse NLP tasks: named entity classification, dependency parsing, and sentence translation. Experimental results confirm that this approach yields improved outcomes in comparison to existing methods, including static word representations.

A comprehensive dataset is crucial for the development of reliable and efficient traffic sign recognition systems, especially in the context of autonomous driving. The availability of diverse datasets is necessary to accommodate diverse environmental conditions and traffic standards. This paper introduces a new dataset, FinTSC, which boasts an extensive collection of over 1 million high-quality images of over 30 distinct traffic sign categories. The dataset is meticulously curated from a range of sources, including human contributors and object detection algorithms, and undergoes rigorous validation and quality checks. The resulting dataset is thoroughly evaluated using established benchmarking methods and made available for public access to foster progress in traffic sign detection and classification.

A widely used method in recommendation systems, collaborative filtering, is often based on user-based or item-based approaches. Although the item-based method using user-item interactions has been improved with negative sampling, this technique has limitations in its ability to utilize the entire interaction dataset effectively. In an attempt to overcome these limitations, we developed a novel framework for self-supervised collaborative filtering. This framework enables a model to learn from its own errors and refine itself in an unsupervised manner by utilizing masked-based or contrastive learning techniques. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of this framework over existing negative sampling methods.

We derive formulas for counting a projective line covered by a generic curve with marked points under specific conditions: when the curve's class is a divisor at $n$ points with negative self-intersection, and when it's a divisor at three distinct, infinitely close points (in the projective case). Our approach utilizes the intersection theory of Chow varieties, enabling us to address related problems such as counting covers of an elliptic curve by a generic curve.

We investigate a gapped Dirac semimetal model and explore its phase transitions by adjusting the Kekule distortion parameters. By using a real-space approach, we demonstrate that the model can have a semimetallic phase under specific conditions of band inversion. This phase can transition into a superconducting or insulating phase depending on the parameters of the band inversion. We have identified the critical boundaries for these phase transitions and demonstrated that the gapped Dirac semimetal model can exhibit a range of distinct phases, including semimetallic, superconducting, insulating VBS, and AKLT phases.

In the context of population dynamics, particularly for models involving the Lotka-Volterra interaction, we explore the existence of canard solutions near the stable equilibrium point $E_3$. Canard solutions serve as a notable phenomenon in two-dimensional differential systems exhibiting a Hopf bifurcation with supercritical or subcritical properties. The presence of canard solutions implies a reversal of the stability properties of the equilibrium point $E_3$. Specifically, we examine the stability of the equilibrium for the two models, one involving the interaction of three species and two predators, and identify its stability at the bifurcation point $E_3$.

The detection of higher order gravitational waves has significant implications for astrophysics and cosmology, and we are investigating a potential new source of diverse gravitational wave spectra found in binary systems. Our study involves analyzing the waveforms generated by the motion of binary bodies, as described by the post-Newtonian formalism, and we are particularly interested in the waveforms produced when the binary's center of mass is not at its nodes. We have developed a method, based on the Regge model, to calculate and match the time and frequency domains of these waveforms, and we are comparing the results to equivalent solutions for a binary neutron star system. Our findings show that the waveforms generated using the Regge model are consistent with those from the Regge-like wave model, and we are now working on extending our analysis to include binary black hole systems as well as waveforms with higher order modes and finite sizes, and we are also developing a method to separate and isolate the different modes present in the waveforms.

The Gaia mission can detect distant stars being pulled by an invisible companion, 
causing their paths to be distorted over time. By tracking these stars and 
measuring the distortions, scientists may be able to find the companion. This 
method is tested using simulated data from the DR2 release. The study finds 
suggestive signs of such distortions in the stars near the Galactic plane. 
Although the current data lacks the accuracy required to confirm the presence 
of long-range gravitational forces. Future releases of Gaia may have the power 
to confirm the existence of these previously hidden companions.

In this paper, we explore the application of a Genetic Algorithm for resolving ill-posed inverse problems in magnetohydrodynamics. To address the inherent limitations of gradient-based methods, such as slow convergence, we employ a novel Genetic Algorithm, capable of overcoming these issues. A comprehensive analysis of the proposed method is provided, including a theoretical discussion underpinning the approach, a proposed mutation operator, and a concise description of the algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the method through numerical experiments, comparing its results with those obtained from a gradient-based least-squares method.

This paper is focused on developing decay estimates for a type of three-variable oscillatory integral, $E_{T}$, defined by the formula
\[ E_T (x,y,z) = \int_{0}^{T} e^{ i (t \cdot (x - 2 \theta \times z - z \times \theta))} \, dt, \; x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \; \; (\theta \in S^2), \]
particularly when the phase function is sufficiently smooth. We derive specific decay estimates for $E_T (x, y, z)$ in $x$ for all $y$ and $z$, and in $z$ for all $x$, with explicit decay rates.

This paper presents an enhanced dataset and an improved model for identifying hate speech, incorporating data augmentation and model ensembles to increase performance stability. Our model, comprising a BERT and RoBERTa combination, outperforms previous studies, achieving specific accuracy rates (76.99%, 76.79%, and 76.59% for Twitter, ta-ds, and ta-all datasets respectively). Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of training a hate speech detector on a smaller dataset before applying it to a larger dataset, achieving a 76.99% accuracy on Twitter data, surpassing the previous ta dataset's best published result.

This research focuses on the reliability of quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) forces as pseudopotential valence charges increase from 8 to 20, employing the diffusion Monte Carlo method within a plane-wave augmented-wave framework. By examining atomic and molecular binding energies, elastic properties, and lattice dynamics for various systems, we assess the accuracy of QMC forces and the computational costs associated with their generation and relaxation. Our research demonstrates that the accuracy of QMC forces can be reliably assessed through a custom elastic constant test, allowing us to identify the valence charge threshold beyond which QMC forces are unreliable, and providing a predictive valence charge range for QMC forces based on existing pseudopotential choices.

Following the 2020 U.S. elections, social media platforms removed content that falsely claimed the election results were manipulated, which led some people to rely on alternative platforms. We examined the spread of election-related misinformation across platforms and investigated how social media moderation actions affected the misinformation spread on these alternative platforms. We found that the spread of false election fraud claims on alternative platforms contributed to a decline in public trust in the election process, which can undermine the democratic election process. Our study also revealed that the deletion of misinformation on the original platforms led to the replication of similar content on alternative platforms, often with minimal modifications. This replication accelerated the spread of misinformation in environments with weaker moderation policies on alternative platforms.

We examine the ensemble of points exhibiting significant pointwise emergence under the influence of Borel potentials for processes driven by random dynamics. For processes that are not only mixing but also satisfy a strong statistical property, we establish a connection between the Hausdorff dimension of highly emergent points and the unstable Hausdorff dimension of the associated hyperbolic measure. This connection is further linked to the lower bound of central Lyapunov exponents and the Hausdorff dimension of periodic points.

Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) are renowned for their capacity to provide uncertainty predictions, yet current BNN training approaches are hindered by high memory requirements and computationally lengthy training cycles. This paper presents a novel, low-cost training algorithm for BNNs that leverages the application of gradient-based optimization techniques to differential equation-based loss functions. This method capitalizes on the local linearity of feedforward neural networks to efficiently improve training performance, ultimately resulting in a significant 10-fold reduction in training time while achieving a 1% increase in test accuracy compared to conventional BNN training methods.

One of the most well-established theories for modeling chemical reactions called the Marcus regime has a major flaw when used for certain types of systems. When these systems are weakly connected, the theory produces inaccurate results, which are due to its underlying assumptions. To address this issue, we've developed a new approach that improves upon an existing theory to provide more accurate predictions for these systems. Our research shows that this new approach is effective for a wide range of systems and significantly reduces errors that occur when making predictions for certain types of chemical reactions. Furthermore, we've confirmed that this new approach is also applicable to a related theory used for certain strong-coupling systems, even when they are weakly connected to other systems. To support these findings, we've created a new software tool that can be used to analyze and make predictions for certain types of chemical reactions.

This paper presents a Bayesian approach to designing trajectory tracking feedback controls that leverage Gaussian Processes to account for system model uncertainties. By using sparse, distributed regression techniques, the method can capture complex interactions and generalize over varying operating conditions without requiring retraining. As a result, the system becomes more adaptable and resilient to parameter variations and changing conditions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using a robotic arm example, showing significant improvements in tracking error and disturbance rejection capacity over a deep neural network-based controller.

Theoretical analysis of the thin-film alloy Fe$_2$V$_{0.8}$W$_{0.2}$Al reveals significant improvements in thermoelectric performance due to reduced electrical resistance caused by magnetic disorder, as predicted by calculations that incorporate magnetism and transport properties. These findings suggest that such alloys could be valuable for future thermoelectric applications.

The subset sum problem, classified as NP-hard in computer science, can be solved efficiently using a new method based on the Grover's algorithm with only 2^log(n) query complexity. In comparison, conventional approaches such as dynamic programming have a higher time complexity of O(2^n.  In this work, we enhance the well-known quantum random access codes method to determine the sum of bits in an n-bit binary number with query efficiency.  Additionally, we apply superdense coding and quantum teleportation to transmit n bits using only 3 log(n) qubits, with possible errors.  Furthermore, we implement quantum random access codes to solve binary search on an n-ary vector in time complexity of O(2^(log(n)/2)).

Given a non-zero element $a$ in $F_q[x]/\langle x^m-a\rangle$, we can construct $a$'s discrete logarithm relative to the base $x^m-1$ in $F_q[x]/\langle x^m-a\rangle$ and $F_q[x]/\langle x^m-1\rangle$. Furthermore, we can calculate the average length of the constructed elements in $F_q[x]/\langle x^m-a\rangle$ for a randomly chosen $a$ within $F_q[x]/\langle x^m-a\rangle$ or $F_q[x]/\langle x^m-1\rangle$.

In recent years, a significant focus has been placed on improving the performance of analysis tools for model checkers like Uppaal through the use of automated code generation techniques. However, this approach relies heavily on a translation process that can be time-consuming and may not always generate optimal code. To overcome these limitations, a new project utilizes the intermediate language of the LLVM compiler to create customized versions of Uppaal's core functions, thereby reducing its runtime complexity. By recompiling Uppaal's core functions, this method aims to minimize the overhead associated with model checking, particularly for large and complex models.

Compressed sensing enables high-quality images to be obtained by utilizing fewer measurements than required by traditional methods, primarily when dealing with systems fundamentally underdetermined. This concept has global applicability across imaging technologies, from radar to magnetic resonance, through the integration of advanced signal processing techniques. This article aims to provide a comprehensive review of the existing knowledge on compressed sensing, focusing on the theoretical aspects, while also exploring its practical implementations and applications in image recovery and estimation tasks. Furthermore, it discusses potential avenues for further research and development in the field of compressed sensing.

We have developed a time-dependent framework for analyzing the quantum motion of photo-electrons generated in two-color, bi-circular laser fields. By employing this approach, we have discovered a unique two-color phenomenon that produces a ring-shaped momentum distribution for the photo-electrons. This effect is characterized by a single, dominant ring that emerges as a result of the interference between the orbital angular momenta of the induced dipoles. We have also investigated the influence of individual laser field parameters on the shape and amplitude of the ring, with a particular focus on the conditions necessary to generate the predicted ring-shaped distribution. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that this phenomenon is robust against variations in laser parameters. Additionally, we have compared our theoretical findings with recent experimental results and have identified the potential for this two-color effect in generating high-order harmonics.

In the context of Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL), the main hurdle lies in properly distinguishing between classes with limited labeled examples. To address this issue, we develop a new SSL method known as Contrastive Label-Contrasting (CLC). CLC works by comparing instances from the same class with each other, thereby forcing the network to differentiate between samples within the same class. To achieve this, we introduce a contrastive loss function that pushes instances together within the same class. To enhance robustness and generalizability, we propose a two-stage training approach that initially trains the model to distinguish between classes and subsequently transfers knowledge to generate pseudo labels for unlabeled data, ultimately refining the model's classification ability. Experimental results demonstrate that CLC outperforms current state-of-the-art SSL techniques.

The measurement of gene expression plays a crucial role in understanding various biological processes. Recent advancements in microarray technology have made it possible to measure expression levels with greater precision and accuracy. However, the traditional Poisson model often fails to provide reliable estimates due to its sensitivity to outliers. In response, we propose a new regularized Poisson model that incorporates data from previous time points to improve gene expression measurements. By analyzing the Fisher information, we show that our model yields more reliable estimates than the standard Poisson model, particularly in handling genes with zero or low expression levels. Through simulations and real-world data analysis, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in gene expression time-series analysis.

In the field of machine learning, semi-supervised learning is crucial when there's a substantial amount of unlabeled data but only scarce amounts of labeled data are available, prompting researchers to explore various methods including graph-based techniques, which model relationships between data points in the feature space, thus being highly effective for classifying nodes in an unsupervised graph as belonging to different classes or labels. This paper presents a novel approach called the "Labeling Graph-based Semi-Supervised Learning Method" (LGSLM) that aims to minimize the number of labels needed for training the semi-supervised learning model by leveraging the structure of the graph. LGSLM has been successfully integrated into the well-established graph-based semi-supervised learning algorithm, Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). The proposed LGSLM-GCN has been tested on the CLEVR Datasets and outperformed other state-of-the-art methods by reducing the required number of labels while maintaining the accuracy.

In the context of Quantum Approximate Optimisation (QAOA), saturation of training refers to a point where further increases in complexity (gates or circuits) do not improve performance. Our study reveals that this saturation point aligns with a method used to calculate optimal depth, and that it can be anticipated without actual training. Additionally, we demonstrate that overtraining QAOA results in predictable degradation, which can be forecasted from the point of saturation using a specific rule of thumb. These findings have practical implications for QAOA's use in computational devices.

Person Re-Identification is a crucial task in surveillance systems that involves identifying individuals across different images from multiple cameras with varying imaging conditions. The challenge requires analyzing both the person's appearance and tracklet patterns while accounting for the effects of missing and imbalanced data distribution. To address these issues, a novel approach called Cross Attention Semantic Topic Adaptation (CASTA), is introduced, combining cross attention networks with a two-stage learning method that adapts semantic topics. The method uses a cross attention network to capture long-term feature relationships between pairs of images and a two-stage learning algorithm that uses initial topic models to transfer knowledge and adapt topics based on discriminative properties. Experimental results on multiple datasets, including Market-1501, DukeMTMC-reID, and DukeMTMC-reID, demonstrate that CASTA outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms.

This study leverages the vast amount of publicly accessible power system data to create a comprehensive dataset for supporting research in this field. By combining and structuring data from two prominent sources, including IEEE test cases and open source solutions, and adding calculated metadata, we address two pressing concerns in power system research: the scarcity of data and its often incompatible format. The resulting dataset, titled 'derivative of TFeOS,' is designed to be easily accessible to researchers who may not have access to original data sets, allowing them to reproduce results, validate new data, and explore additional research avenues.

Our study involves employing a recursive technique to investigate the existence of 
fixed points and variational inequality solutions for mappings that have a certain 
upper semicontinuity property, also known as $U$-mappings. We derive new 
existence theorems for these mappings that remain in the class of $U$-mappings at each step of the recursive process.

The set of axes for hyperbolic elements within a Fuchsian group uniquely corresponds to its commensurability class, thereby constituting its defining characteristic. This particular property, however, is not unique to Fuchsian groups, as any co-compact hyperbolic geometric category will possess the same characteristic. This discovery is rooted in the concept that any such category can be broken down into a product of its Fuchsian groups and its commensurability class is solely determined by the collection of Sl(2,ℝ) orbits of axes in the category. For brevity, this description will be referred to as the axes spectrum. The axes spectrum is a topological invariant for non-cocompact groups, but it loses its distinctiveness when dealing with cocompact groups, necessitating a more refined understanding of its properties.

We are investigating lepton flavor violation within the context of decays involving Higgs bosons into three leptons and similar processes involving $Z$ and chargino/neutralino particles. Specifically, we are considering scenarios where neutralino, chargino, and slepton masses vary based on specific SUSY breaking scenarios while Higgs mass is determined through radiative corrections in the heavy top quark mass hypothesis. Our analysis delves into the potential implications of upcoming experiments such as the Belle II collider and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for uncovering LFV phenomena in supersymmetric particle physics theories.

Our investigation focused on the impact of hydrostatic pressure on the electronic properties of Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ single crystals, specifically those with x = 0 and 0.1, using electrical transport, magnetoresistance, and thermal transport measurements under pressure. These studies revealed that applying pressure causes a significant increase in resistivity, accompanied by a notable decrease in magnetoresistance, and leads to a positive thermal anomaly at low temperatures, indicating a phase transition. Our findings suggest that Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ undergoes a superconducting phase shift at a relatively low transition temperature, and that this transition can be triggered by applied pressure.

The phenomenon of black hole evaporation through Hawking radiation is being revisited in the context of causal horizon methods. This reevaluation is focused on recovering information from black holes and matching the standard Hawking or Unruh effect for an observer outside the event horizon. Additionally, our methods are applied to quantify the rate of information retrieval in the Hawking radiation process. Furthermore, unitarity of the evaporation process is analyzed through a complementary channel's entanglement entropy, which we calculate using causal horizon methods.

In physical process data collection, noise contamination is a significant problem, and a new filtering approach in time-domain is proposed to address this. A novel inverse filter, grounded in the principles of the Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, is designed to filter out noise and ensure data accuracy. This filter incorporates the spatial properties of the data, distinguishing it from conventional low-pass filters that rely on time-only characteristics. By employing this filter, the method maintains data's temporal smoothness naturally. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness in removing random noise is validated through numerical experiments with synthetic and real-world data, and further analysis is provided to elucidate the effects of spatial regularization parameters on the filtered results.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to navigation through uncharted territories, built upon the principles of the Q-learning algorithm in conjunction with the self-organizing map and long-term memory retention mechanism. By integrating memory components into Q-learning, the proposed method aims to enhance long-term memory for navigation by drawing upon previously learned experiences. To achieve this, the method employs two distinct memory types: topographic and temporal memory. The topographic memory, modeled as a self-organizing map, is utilized to store diverse environmental features, while the temporal memory, represented by an external memory buffer, enables the recording of recent experiences. To further refine the temporal memory, a reinforcement learning-based policy is implemented to select the most relevant experiences for storage. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to a novel, self-designed 2D environment with the goal of reaching a target using a custom-built robotic vehicle. The results of the experiments reveal the significant role of long-term memory in the method's performance, especially in the long-term navigation phase, where the method outperforms existing approaches.

Recent studies have shown that large pre-trained language models can achieve impressive performance in various downstream tasks through fine-tuning with minimal data, yet they struggle to adapt to novel and unfamiliar tasks. To overcome this limitation, our research introduces a novel approach called instruction-tuning, which enables large models to learn new tasks from scratch through the use of brief, task-oriented prompts. By fine-tuning large models on these prompts, our approach significantly enhances the models' ability to generalize to unseen tasks, surpassing current state-of-the-art results on the SuperGLUE benchmark and demonstrating promising outcomes on HELLAS benchmark tasks. Furthermore, we found that the success of instruction-tuning is largely due to the underlying structure of the training data, rather than the sheer volume of data used, indicating a promising path forward for developing flexible and adaptable language models.

Despite the widespread growth of online learning communities over the past decade, there is still a lack of comprehensive understanding about the role of these informal learning environments in supporting the acquisition of new knowledge and skills. In our research, we conducted a detailed examination of 17 diverse online learning communities and discovered that they serve as effective venues for learning and skill development, although each community has its own unique focus. Three primary objectives for learning were identified - exploring concepts, acquiring practical knowledge, and sharing expertise - which are pursued through distinct collaborative strategies. These findings can help inform designers of online learning environments and provide them with valuable insights for creating community experiences that effectively support casual learners' pursuit of knowledge.

A new computational method for calculating high density $E_2$ correlation energy in the uniform electron gas has been developed. This method uses a combination of model wave functions, including those derived from the Hartree-Fock theory and the model wave function of Lam and Kohn, to generate an iterative equation for $E_2$. These computations, which involve the solution of a non-linear integral equation, yield results in good agreement with the exact solution. Specifically, for a range of densities, the calculated $E_2$ values are within 10% of the exact solution.

In 1991, Brenier proved a significant theorem establishing a unique relationship between the difference of two positive density fields and a specific vector field, which is now commonly referred to as the Brenier map. This breakthrough discovery has had a profound impact on the field of optimal transport and has been a driving force behind its development in the past few decades. The Brenier theorem has far-reaching applications in the design of algorithms for computing optimal transport maps in practice. A recent study by Madry et al. utilized the Brenier map for the stable computation of multi-marginal optimal transport, which is now known as Madry transport. This algorithm has been widely used in machine learning for the tasks of density estimation and data generation. However, Brenier transport has been limited in its application to small datasets and datasets with specific distribution properties. This study presents a new approach called generalized Madry transport, which can be applied to a broader class of problems. The approach is based on a new theorem that provides a characterization of the difference of arbitrary measures with finite second moments, which is now known as the second moment theorem. The approach is based on a new algorithm for computing generalized optimal transport, which is now known as the G-Madry algorithm. The approach is shown to be a generalization of the Brenier map and is shown to be related to a new algorithm for the stable computation of multi-marginal optimal transport, which is now known as generalized Madry transport. In recent years, a growing number of studies have highlighted the significant risks associated with massive data breaches due to widespread data thefts. As a result, there is an increasing emphasis on developing secure data protection systems. This paper presents a groundbreaking approach to safeguarding data, involving the utilization of tensor network representations of physical systems, encompassing quantum fields, condensed matter physics, particle physics, and its application in protecting big data. The proposed framework leverages the fact that tensor networks inherently possess inherent characteristics that ensure data confidentiality. The presented findings demonstrate that tensor networks, specifically graph-based networks, can effectively safeguard sensitive information, rendering it virtually unusable, even with the acquisition of extensive data. The research showcases the efficacy of tensor networks in maintaining data privacy, exemplified by the utilization of data compression algorithms. The study also reveals the resilience of tensor networks against data breaches, even when the acquisition of minor data is possible. Furthermore, a novel, decentralized architecture is introduced, featuring a distributed processing of data samples. The proposed solution is evaluated using actual data sets, featuring a high degree of diversity, encompassing images, audio, and videos. The results indicate that the presented method surpasses existing data protection techniques, such as federated learning and secure aggregation, by achieving superior performance. The study also highlights the potential of tensor networks in modeling complex physical systems, exemplified by the application in modeling the human brain.

When policies learned in simulated environments are transferred to real-world robots, 
they often don't work as expected, due to the discrepancy between the simulated and 
real-world dynamics. This paper proposes a model-based reinforcement learning method 
that uses a dynamics model to adjust policy updates and account for the simulation-to-reality 
discrepancy online. The method, called Sim2Real RL, employs model-based policy optimisation 
to adapt to real-world dynamics. Experimental results on a 6-legged robot demonstrate that 
Sim2Real RL outperforms existing transfer techniques in both stationary and moving 
environment settings.

The study of jet interactions with the interstellar medium holds the key to understanding the relationship between galaxy evolution, black hole growth, and star formation. Nuclei with dual jets provide a unique opportunity to investigate the connection between jet physics and environment. This research presents a comprehensive analysis of the dual-jet galaxy NGC 3256, focusing on its nuclear properties. Observations using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array and the Hubble Space Telescope reveal a complex nuclear environment with a high star formation rate and significant gas inflows. We have identified dual-jet structures, molecular outflows, and ionized outflows originating from the nucleus, as well as a large-scale galaxy-wide ionized outflow. This galaxy is characterized by a high efficiency of energy conversion from mechanical to radiative energy, suggesting a strong connection between jet activity and molecular gas. Our findings imply that the dual jets in NGC 3256 are likely fueled by a central black hole. This galaxy's unique environment, with a high star formation rate and molecular gas content, may be conducive to jet growth and environmental effects, such as fueling molecular outflows and driving large-scale ionized outflows.

This study introduces a nonparametric estimation method for variable coefficients within a time series framework, allowing the coefficients to change over time in an arbitrary manner. By utilizing a sieve for coefficient function space, we achieve consistency in our estimator, even when the coefficients have a slow rate of convergence. We also derive an asymptotic normality result for our estimator, even when the coefficients have a constant rate of convergence but the noise has a slow rate. Importantly, our estimator is the first that can handle time-varying coefficients and is applicable to a broad class of time series models, both linear and nonlinear, without making specific assumptions about the coefficients. In addition, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our estimator through simulations and an application to real-world data.

This paper presents the approach and outcomes of the team from Aasvark by identifying and categorizing offensive language and content that is highly offensive. For this task, we employed cutting-edge models including BERT and distillation models (BERT-DFM), as well as conventional n-gram-based classifiers (RNN and SVM). In addition, we explored the effectiveness of transfer learning by utilizing pre-trained models trained on English data (BMCC, MSC), yet fine-tuned on the specific dataset. Our team's solution ranked 7th out of 23 contributing teams, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.9136.

Research on brain function through functional connectivity has been utilized to understand various psychiatric and neurological disorders such as schizophrenia, which is linked to disrupted brain connectivity. Utilizing data-driven methods like deep learning has been shown to uncover intricate relationships in the brain. Nonetheless, deep learning models heavily rely on data input design and the quality, necessitating a deeper understanding of the brain's structure and the disorder's underlying causes. We present a novel deep learning approach that generates data through a neural network model, incorporating a residual graph convolutional encoder-decoder architecture. This is trained using a dual loss function comprising graph autoencoder and graph convolutional classification layers. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method by generating high-quality connectivity matrices and classifying subjects accurately, including those with severe forms of schizophrenia.

This study applies the three times accelerated Kish method to find minimizers that lie outside the scope of the loss function, without violating convergence. Building on Nesterov's accelerated method, our improvement maintains the original convergence rate while incorporating the Kish acceleration.

This research examines the application of implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta (IMEX) methods to solve systems of hyperbolic equations, with components having variable and time-dependent coefficients. It presents comprehensive findings on the necessary conditions for convergence, along with associated convergence rates, applicable to systems of $m$ equations with $N$ spatial dimensions. By leveraging the maximum norms of the variables, an accurate and adaptable analysis is conducted, taking into account the variable coefficients and nonlinear source terms. It is demonstrated that IMEX methods with explicit-steps of $4^{th}$ or higher order and implicit-steps of $2^{nd}$ or higher order achieve $2m$-wise convergence at the rate of $2m/3$. Furthermore, it is discovered that explicit-steps of $3^{rd}$ order and implicit-steps of $2^{nd}$ order attains $2m$-wise convergence at the rate of $4/5$. This study also investigates the stability of solutions in relation to initial conditions and provides optimal error bounds. It is further extended to the context of semi-discrete systems, and it is shown that the findings can be applied to the systems of conservation laws with variable and time-dependent coefficients. It is also demonstrated that the established results are applicable to the systems of hyperbolic equations with variable and time-dependent coefficients, and these findings are validated by numerical experiments.

Achieving higher energy conversion efficiency while minimizing losses is a key goal in solar cell research.  One strategy to achieve this is by employing a photonic band-gap crystal as a back reflector instead of a metal reflector, which could reduce reflection losses.  To investigate this approach, a theoretical model was developed to compare the performance of a metal back reflector and a photonic band-gap crystal back reflector in thin-film silicon solar cells, taking into account their effects on absorption and recombination losses.  The results showed that the photonic band-gap crystal back reflector can lead to minor improvements in efficiency, but primarily through reductions in reflection losses.  However, these gains are limited by the optical coupling loss associated with the crystal's thickness and the frequency response of the crystal.  Furthermore, this study also reveals that the performance of a metal back reflector can be matched or exceeded by a properly designed photonic band-gap crystal back reflector, provided it can effectively reestablish optical coupling upon multiple reflections.

Credal sets enable uncertain knowledge to be represented within a solution space, while set-valued optimization problem-based approaches facilitate the conversion of this uncertainty into practical consequences under various probabilistic criteria. This research paper investigates the application of credal sets to a type of nonlinear optimization problem with a limited range, utilizing a convex quadratic programming relaxation. By leveraging duality and linear algebra properties, we derive a straightforward method for calculating the credal set representation of the solution space, which is then verified through numerical testing using a real-world energy management scenario.

Matrix factorization and deep learning have been widely used for user preference modeling, yet they are limited in capturing the complex user behavior. To overcome this, researchers have introduced graph neural networks (GNNs) into the recommendation domain, but current methods have fallen short in explaining their predictions. To address this issue, a new algorithm is proposed that combines GNNs with BART, a BERT variant, to develop a Bayesian BART (BBART) model for user preference modeling. In this algorithm, a BART encoder is utilized to learn preferences and a GNN is employed to learn explainable latent factors. A Bayesian approach is employed to simultaneously infer the model's parameters and the uncertainty in the recommendations. Experimental results on multiple datasets show that BBART achieves superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods while providing accurate recommendation uncertainty estimates.

The eternally non-Markovian Pauli channel serves as a model of a quantum channel that has a finite dimension and non-decreasing qubit error rates over time, yet still exhibits non-Markovian characteristics. Although the eternally non-Markovian Pauli channel appears to defy a physical counterpart, it can be represented as the outcome of a continuous measurement process based on a continuous quantum variable. We demonstrate that the channel's behavior can be understood in terms of the conditional states resulting from this measurement process. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the channel's non-Markovian traits stem from the fact that the Hermitian operators associated with the measurement process have a non-decreasing overlap with the initial state over time, a phenomenon that can be observed across a broad class of non-Markovian channels.

Enhancing the efficacy of supervised tabular models necessitates leveraging data augmentation, yet tabular data augmentation poses a unique challenge due to its inherent domain-specificity. This problem is exacerbated by the lack of a standardized set of domain-agnostic transformations, like image or text augmentation, which can be applied to tabular data. Consequently, creating domain-specific augmentations necessitates substantial expertise in a particular domain. This paper introduces a novel, flexible, and domain-agnostic approach to tabular data augmentation that is based on a combination of row splitting and stacking techniques. This innovative method allows for the reuse of domain-agnostic cell and row-level transformations to generate a wide variety of domain-specific tabular data augmentations. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that these domain-specific augmentations can be utilized to enhance the efficacy of supervised tabular models without requiring any domain-specific knowledge.

Developing a semantic map, which translates spoken language into visual cues, enables robots to comprehend human commands and execute them in real-world settings. This paper focuses on creating a semantic map that allows robots to assemble items based on user instructions. Our solution integrates multiple speech recognition techniques and uses a graph-based algorithm to identify the required objects and actions for assembly tasks. Furthermore, we implement a navigation system that directs the robot to the necessary locations within a 3D environment to carry out the user-specified actions. Our proposed system is successfully demonstrated and tested in a simulated environment.

Rikudo is a number placement puzzle in which the player is tasked with rearranging tiles to create a specified pattern.  By focusing on a simplified version of this game, we demonstrate its inherent complexity, proving that Rikudo is both NP hard and in the class PSPACE.  A key proof of this is achieved through a reduction of a solvable puzzle, Sudoku, to Rikudo, thereby establishing Rikudo as PSPACE complete.  Additionally, the study shows that, in order to solve any simplified Rikudo configuration, the player must employ space that scales at least poly-space, even when allowing for the possibility of making an infinite number of moves.  This analysis highlights the relationship between game complexity and the player's requirements for space and time, as well as providing a foundation for further research into the puzzle's broader theoretical implications.

The classic OT problem, framed as a linear programming issue, poses computational obstacles for machine learning purposes, particularly in terms of large-scale optimization and sparse-convexity. To tackle these issues, entropic regularization has been utilized, although this approach leads to a probabilistic distribution of transport plans. This can be mitigated by introducing additional penalties in the optimization objective. We focus on a recently developed method of regularization that introduces term penalties on norms of transport plans, balancing the trade-off between optimization and sparsity. We examine conditions that ensure the resulting optimization problem has a unique global minimum and, under certain conditions, this minimum corresponds to a unique, most sparsensable transport plan. We also investigate the first-order optimality conditions for this minimum, providing a method to test for sparsity. We test our theory through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, observing an interesting link between sparsity and norm penalties.

This paper explores the connection between Hecke groups, modular equations, and Ramanujan's formulas, specifically the expressions for the values of elliptic modular forms. We establish that Hecke groups provide a comprehensive framework for understanding modular equations, demonstrating that the solutions to these equations correspond to the eigenvalues of the automorphisms associated with the Hecke groups.

The detailed study of quasar-galaxy lens system spectra has significantly 
improved our understanding of the mass distribution within galaxy dark matter 
halos and the characteristics of the surrounding medium. 
However, the observation of these spectra is often complicated by the 
contamination of foreground and background light paths. 
To overcome this issue, we have developed a new method that utilizes principal 
component analysis to extract high-signal-to-noise ratio deflector galaxy 
spectra from mixed quasar-host-galaxy light. Our approach was applied to 
spectra from the SDSS-DR7 spectroscopic database, resulting in the 
identification of 143 quasar-galaxy lens systems with newly extracted deflector 
galaxy spectra. Our method was validated through the analysis of nearby quasar-galaxy 
lens systems for which high-quality deflector spectra were previously observed. 
Our findings have the potential to greatly enhance future studies of quasar-galaxy 
lens systems, particularly when combined with future, more extensive spectroscopic 
surveys.

Our investigation focuses on the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the $q$-fractional differential equation, as well as its dependence on initial conditions. We also examine the continuous dependence of solutions on their associated initial values, and apply our findings to two applications: the nonlocal $q$-fractional $k$-Laplacian problem and the jump differential equation with a nonlinear singular right-hand side.

In a significant departure from conventional theories, recent research indicates that non-magnetic, dielectric materials can transmit thermal conductivity in the form of a Hall effect, which was previously thought to be exclusive to magnetic materials. This breakthrough suggests that the thermal conductivity in these materials is linked to a non-zero Berry curvature, which is distinct from the Berry curvature associated with electric properties. This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the origin of the Hall effect in these materials, which is rooted in the unique interaction between lattice vibrations and electronic states. Furthermore, our research identifies certain material parameters that are crucial to this phenomenon, which can be experimentally verified.

A one-shot Raman imaging approach utilizing second harmonic generation (SHG) images is proposed. An alternative to traditional pump laser fluorescence imaging, this method leverages the spatial sensitivity of SHG images to localize the Raman signal. Similar to nonlinear microscopy techniques, this technique exploits the distinct SHG image contrast to differentiate sample structures. A proof-of-concept experiment is conducted using a commercial multichannel camera and a commercial inverted microscope, which captures SHG images of a USAF target and sample with no SHG activity. Following deconvolution of the SHG images, Raman images are reconstructed with approximately 10 times higher resolution than traditional one-shot Raman imaging. Furthermore, this method eliminates autofluorescence and background signals through the application of a nonlinear optical image deconvolution algorithm.

This article explores matrix analogues of Fejér and Levin-Stečkin inequalities, with matrices considered to be polynomials of algebraic functions. Associated matrix polynomials are characterized by a multi-parameter family, with distinct parameters influencing distinct polynomial sets, resulting in distinct matrix families. Fejér and Levin-Stečkin matrix inequalities are proven using a multi-parameter matrix perspective, with matrix polynomials being derived from this framework.

In investigating the properties of area increase during black hole evaporation, we have found a distinct characteristic of the boundary black hole horizon when a system undergoes a black hole evaporation process. We have observed that as long as the area of the boundary black hole decreases, the point of the boundary black hole horizon will experience an unusual phenomenon known as the Markov process. This phenomenon is described in detail in terms of the associated semigroup of Markov matrices, the detailed-flux boundary condition, and the transition probability between different points at the boundary black hole horizon. We have also explored the properties of the Markov process in terms of the semigroup of matrices, the transition probability matrix, and the characteristic polynomial of the matrix.

A novel method is developed to distinguish between descendant states of two-dimensional Conformal Field Theory, specifically through correlations in space-time rather than time. This approach involves analyzing the spatial correlations of an arbitrary number of CFT operators, which can be either local or time-dependent, and calculating various entanglement entropies. Key results include explicit formulas for entropies, proof of monotonicity, and derivation of Virasoro primary operators' entanglement entropy as a function of screening dimensions. Furthermore, the method is applied to the Ising model, 3D XY model, and Majumdar-Shubin model, and demonstrates agreement with known results.

To assess the performance of control systems and evaluate the efficacy of cybersecurity solutions, researchers utilize Industrial Control System (ICS) testbeds. These facilities allow for the collective testing of control systems, communication networks, and security measures within a shared platform. This paper presents ICS-OR, a comprehensive software or firm-ware testbed that supports both physical and virtual environments. Its architecture leverages container technology to ensure secure sharing of ICS assets during shared-use evaluations. Notably, ICS-OR is the first open-source testbed of its kind and is designed to be easily adaptable to various hardware configurations. Its modular architecture also enables the seamless integration of new features and components.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning techniques that employ linear or monotonic value decomposition to achieve separate optimization for each agent overlook a critical constraint affecting these approaches, leading to undesirable outcomes. Our research reveals that methods relying on linear or monotonic decomposition inherently limit the range of an agent's policy representation, thereby rendering some policies incapable of interacting with the other agents within the environment. Consequently, this limitation reduces the effectiveness of these approaches. Furthermore, our experiments confirm that this constraint applies to a broader range of policy representation methods, including linear and monotonic ones. We also demonstrate that this constraint can be overcome by introducing an additional penalty term in the objective function, thus expanding the range of available policies for the agents.

A stereotype is a widely held, simplified view that is often false, and can harm specific groups if allowed to persist without correction, as such views can spread through social interaction like the spread of viruses. To combat this, we explore the use of automated systems to detect and correct stereotypes within large text datasets. This research addresses two key issues: first, we developed methods to identify and quantify stereotypes in texts without needing to create custom databases or dictionaries of stereotypical terms, and second, as simply detecting stereotypes is not enough, we also need to mitigate their impact by producing counterfactual texts that promote more inclusive perspectives. This research contributes to filling a knowledge gap by introducing an accessible platform for studying stereotypes, providing innovative methods for detecting and countering them, and supporting research in the field of Natural Language Processing.

We investigate an optimization problem to optimize remote electrical tilt in cellular networks through intelligent reflection assistance. The goal is to identify the optimal baseband transmission coefficients for each tower that allow for joint coverage of all required areas while minimizing the total power output. To tackle this challenging optimization task, we present a novel algorithm that employs a layered, nested, fixed point method. The algorithm iteratively refines the bounds of each tower's transmission coefficients by exploiting the problem's multi-quadrant nature. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms current optimization methods, yielding up to 20 dB improvement in power reduction.

The pattern of particle decay in the presence of CP violation is used to calculate the CKM angle gamma with greater precision by combining data from B and Ba decays. Data from 3.0 fb^-1 of LHCb experiment's Run~1 and 1.6 fb^-1 of Run~2, as well as 6.1 pb^-1 of Run~1, was used for the calculation. The calculated CKM angle gamma has an axis at 58.9 degrees, with an error margin of 1.0 degrees, combining various types of particle decay measurements, as well as providing information on flavor.

Several properties of complex ellipsoids among convex bodies in n-dimensional space have been rigorously established in their classical forms. For complex ellipsoids in this space, we demonstrate their key geometric attributes – being smooth bodies with curved surfaces made up of smooth curves. Additionally, we derive the inequality for the Miller--Moeckel--Cohn two-body energy, and prove that complex ellipsoids in this space are uniquely defined by satisfying both of these conditions collectively.

The collection of data without consent is a widespread issue affecting both ordinary individuals and specialized groups such as students and medical patients. As a result of filling out online surveys and providing personal information, they are contributing significantly to the development of machine learning models used in applications like risk assessment. A recent study involving in-person interviews with a diverse group of 79 people found that the majority strongly oppose current data collection methods, particularly those without their consent or awareness. Their concerns centered around the potential for model bias and the lack of control over their data. Based on these findings, there is a strong sentiment among participants that individuals should have more control over their data, leading to a greater willingness to adopt technologies that prioritize consent and protect user privacy.

This research paper explores the application of an optimization technique called K-means clustering to binary Faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling for multiuser multiple-input multiple-output communication systems. The proposed clustering method aims to maximize weighted sum spectral efficiency while adhering to the Nyquist criterion. Notably, it surpasses the performance of existing methods, such as the Gaussian mixture model, particularly when data is binary. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that K-means clustering outperforms Gaussian mixture model and a deep learning-based approach, both in terms of weighted sum spectral efficiency and user count, even surpassing suboptimal FTN signaling schemes.

This study focuses on two key concepts: complete atomic lattices with certain continuity properties under their least upper bounds and greatest integer operations; and continuous lattice structures with specific algebraic characteristics, including distributivity and commutativity. We explore their inherent properties, including substructures, monotone mappings, and completion processes. Notably, we demonstrate the existence of continuous lattice effect algebras with specific algebraic properties, as well as introducing the notion of continuous effect algebras with certain continuity properties under their least upper bounds and greatest integer operations. We also examine continuous effect algebras with these properties and their corresponding continuous lattice counterparts.

This paper presents SaliencyMix, a novel data augmentation technique for improving the saliency detection capability of deep learning models. An essential aspect of saliency detection is identifying the most critical regions of an image, and recent research has shown that training deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with data that highlights these areas significantly enhances their ability to detect salient objects. However, current methods of saliency-aware data augmentation have limitations, and in this context, we introduce SaliencyMix to address these shortcomings. SaliencyMix is a straightforward yet effective data augmentation strategy that involves mixing the original image with saliency maps in a local manner, and the approach is easily applicable to any saliocracy-aware model. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of SaliencyMix by integrating it into existing data augmentation methods, and the experiments show that incorporating SaliencyMix improves the performance of state-of-the-art models on five benchmark datasets. The code for SaliencyMix is available at https://github.com/satryam-mishra/SaliencyMix.

Groups of 2x2 real matrices with specific constraints on their elements are considered and their respective groups of bi-invariant functions with compact support are defined. These bi-invariant functions form convolution algebras that resemble the compact quantum group $O_n$ and $SP_q(n)\otimes O_n$.

Galaxy distributions are affected by a combination of intrinsic alignments (IA) and gravitational lensing. To make progress in separating the two effects using upcoming surveys, controlled simulations are necessary. We have developed a new cosmological simulation suite called the Cosmic IA simulations, allowing us to study the effects of galaxy-galaxy lensing and shear correlations independently. In this paper, we investigate the impact of intrinsic shape correlations on the interpretation of cosmic shear surveys by utilizing the first release of the Cosmic IA simulations, focusing on the intrinsic correlation strength and its influence on the results. We have found that intrinsic correlations can significantly affect the results of shear surveys, especially when considering the correlation between intrinsic shapes and their environment.
